utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we continue, there are a couple of matters I would like to deal first. Good morning, everyone, first. The Chamber will first turn back to the accused's "Motion to preclude the questioning of Momcilo Krajisnik on statements made in parliament," filed on the 4th of November. The Chamber notes that, having heard the parties' further oral submissions yesterday, it considers it important to give its position on the motion prior to the start of Mr. Krajisnik's testimony. The Chamber considers that the accused has failed to demonstrate in the motion and the further oral submissions that while immunities and privileges may protect parliamentary statements in domestic jurisdictions, this applies in international criminal proceedings. The Chamber, therefore, denies the motion. Second, Mr. Tieger, while -- although Mr. Nicholls is not with us, I raised with the parties as to the admitting or tendering some parts of witness interviews with Mr. Tomo Kovac. Where are we in terms of that item? Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, Mr. Nicholls sent me that afternoon a list of proposed excerpts. I objected to several of them. I copied the Chamber on my e-mail back to him, indicating which ones I objected to and why, and we haven't had anything since then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As the Court impliedly noted, it may be preferable to have Mr. Nicholls join us for this discussion. But I was aware that Mr. Nicholls sent the proposed list to Mr. Robinson virtually immediately. I was also aware that Mr. Robinson had raised certain objections. I reviewed quickly some of those objections which I considered to contravene the practice of this Court and the directions insofar as it appeared that -- and I thought they were also factually inaccurate in that he objected supposedly to material that had been read out even though it had not been read out in full. But more importantly, the practice of this Court to my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. I'm sorry to interrupt. Shall we deal with it after the break, first thing after the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think that's fine. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So I would like to deal with it while our memory is fresh. Yes, Mr. Krajisnik, could you make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable. Mr. Robinson, the Chamber requested your -- granted your request for Mr. Krajisnik's counsel to be present today. What happened to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, Mr. Krajisnik was not among the witnesses for whom we had made that request. Since he's not detained, he falls into the category of people that you previously held are not entitled to have counsel present for their testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I should stand corrected. Mr. Krajisnik, before you commence your evidence, I must let you know about this. You heard that the Chamber denied the motion to preclude the questioning on the statements made in parliament, and I take it you are well aware of this but I'd like to explain about the rule of evidence that we have here at the Tribunal, that is, Rule 90(E). Under this rule you may object to answering any question from the accused, Mr. Karadzic, the Prosecutor, or even from us, the Judges, if you believe that your answer might incriminate you in a criminal offence. In this context, "incriminate" means saying something that might amount to an admission of guilt for a criminal offence or saying something that might provide evidence that you might have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that your answer might incriminate you and, as a consequence, you refuse to answer the question, I must let you know that the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question. But in that situation, the Tribunal would ensure that your testimony compelled under such circumstances would not be used in any case that might be laid against you for any offence, save and except the offence of giving false testimony. Do you understand what I have just told you, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Excellencies. Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I cannot avoid these basic initial questions, so please tell us your full name, your father's name, date and place of birth.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: My name is Momcilo Krajisnik, born 22nd January 1945, in Zabrdje near Sarajevo. My father's name is Sretko, mother's name Milka, and I lived in Zabrdje until the end of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, after which I lived as a refugee in Pale, which is a small place near Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us, equally concisely, about your education and career.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: I finished primary school, secondary school, and the school of economics, as well as my post-graduate studies in Sarajevo. After graduating from university in 1968, on the 15th of October that year I found a job in a large company called Energoinvest, and in two sections of that company I worked until the end of 1990 when I was elected MP to the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I was elected Speaker of the Assembly by a majority vote of all parties from all ethnic communities, and stayed in that post until the end. I was actually not occupying that post from the beginning of the war. On the 24th October 1991, I was elected Speaker of the Assembly of the Serbian People of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which later changed its name to the National Assembly of Republika Srpska, and I remained in that position until the end of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. After the end of the war, I was elected member of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina from Republika Srpska, and in -- my first term was after the signing of the Dayton Accords. In 1991, my tenure finished and then I engaged in private business. At that time I started my doctoral thesis. However, on the 3rd of April, 2000, I was arrested, sent to the prison in The Hague, where I spent a little more than nine years. And after the final judgement I was transferred to a jail in the UK. In February 2013, by decision of the President of this Tribunal, I was released. But during my stay in prison I worked actively to collect evidence for a review of my judgement, and I'm very grateful to this Chamber as well because they enabled me to get hold of a large number of documents as well as other services, including the OTP, who are my opponent in these proceedings. They also enabled me to get a large number of documents. Now I live as a refugee and I'm waiting to the great day when I will finally hear the words "not guilty." I see the best two Prosecutors in this Tribunal in my mind's eye, Mr. Tieger and Mr. Kremer, raise the white flag.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you at any point president of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I know I need to leave a pause. In my two-years' term, although I was one of the three equal members of the Presidency, I was never the president because the decision was that the president may be only a representative of the Muslim people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what is the practice now?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: The practice now is rotation in the Presidency; however, during my term of office this principle did not apply.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell the Trial Chamber briefly since when we have known each other, how we met, and the course of our friendship until 1990 when the Serbian Democratic Party was established?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: One day, a friend asked me for an explanation as an economist how loans can be obtained and used from banks. I asked: Why? And he said: I have a friend who needs this information because he wants to start a private business. And he didn't understand my explanation well obviously because he's a poet, so he asked me to find some time and explain it directly to his friend and that friend was Dr. Radovan Karadzic. That was my first encounter with you, Mr. Karadzic. And talking to him, I found out that Dr. Karadzic is part of Sarajevo's intellectual elite and I had an interest in these people, but I didn't know them. And through various private encounters and celebrations of our patron saint's day I got to know many of these people in the elite. I spoke to Mr. Karadzic and those other people about topics that were very interesting at the time. Everybody in Bosnia-Herzegovina was into politics at that time. We talked about various topical issues and inter-ethnic relations, et cetera, and we got to know each better. We became closer. Also because in one trial in Bosnia-Herzegovina we were indicted together and chased out. After four and a half years we were acquitted, however. It was a relapse of one policy in Bosnia-Herzegovina, whereby political opponents were persecuted and prosecuted. When the process began to organise ourselves politically and set up the authorities in Bosnia-Herzegovina, we split briefly because I didn't want to engage in politics. And Dr. Karadzic, too, did not agree to lead a political party. My desire was to help as much as I can from the sidelines, so I was not directly involved in those first early days of the Serbian Democratic Party. I remained an observer. But later I got involved in a peripheral way and it so happens that I was one of the candidates for a member of the Assembly and later I was elected MP.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How did you first start as a back-up candidate and how did you find your way into the Assembly eventually?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: The people who knew me believed that, with my approach, I can be of assistance in organising the situation in a rather disorderly municipality where I lived, which is Novi Grad. And after public appearances on radio and television, I went to the Municipal Board, where human relations were very disturbed. I managed to reconcile the parties, and the ratio in the government was 30 per cent Serbs and 70 per cent others. Since I didn't want to be actively involved in politics, I first refused to be a candidate; however, pressure was exerted on me and I found a compromise solution. I suggested that Professor Unkovic be the first candidate and I was the back-up candidate. When our ticket was discussed at the personnel committee, they didn't know him, Professor Unkovic, but they knew me because of some articles that had appeared in newspapers. So I was better known, and eventually I was put on the ticket for the Sarajevo-Romanija region. Five or six candidates were elected first, and in the early stage I was not. Since many parties did not find their way into the parliament, when the remaining votes were split among other parties, I got one of those spots in the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How did it come about that you were elected by all parties, by majority votes, Speaker of the Bosnia-Herzegovina parliament?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Well, the answer is very short: I was elected as Krajisnik, a man from Krajina, from Sarajevo. Why? Because one region in Bosnia-Herzegovina is called Krajina, and a candidate of the Serbian Democratic Party, candidate for Speaker, was Milan Trbojevic. However, people from Krajina demanded Krajisnik and people from Sarajevo wanted it to be a man from Sarajevo, so it had to be one of the two. And after a very long debate, a solution was still not found, and finally I was elected as a Krajisnik from Sarajevo and that is the only real truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Trial Chamber what your last name means so that we can understand what you just said?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: My last name, Krajisnik, originally means a soldier defending the border, which in Serbian is also called "kraj," boundary. At the time of the Austro-Hungarian and Ottoman Empires, these two great empires kept Serbs on the border who guarded the borders of the empire. And the Serbs who were manning the border as defenders since they were on the edge of the empire, again kraj, edge, border, and my family was one of those, they were named Krajisnik. And I was accepted, approved, by both those who wanted it to be a Krajisnik and those who wanted it to be a man from Sarajevo as a Speaker.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How did you understand, how did you see, the strategic options of the Serbian Democratic Party and what were the strategic options of other parties before the elections, before we came into power?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: All the parties, except those with a communist orientation, wanted a multi-party system in order to introduce democracy in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Because communism had prevailed for a long time and it had many shortcomings and people wanted change. The Serbian Democratic Party of which I was a member and the Party of Democratic Action, SDA, which was a Muslim party, wanted Yugoslavia to continue. And they wanted democracy to be introduced. They wanted a reasonable Federation, and we all worked for Bosnia-Herzegovina to obtain as many privileges and rights as possible because that's where we lived. The Croatian party was HDZ, the Croatian Democratic Union, and it was more geared towards the interests of Croats in Croatia than those in Bosnia-Herzegovina. But when it came to our internal inter-party relations, we were rather close to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How did the first democratic elections in Bosnia-Herzegovina run and who won seats in the parliament?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: After a long communist rule, the parties were nation-based. At that time there were no nationalist parties. Nation-based parties received maximum support of their ethnic communities. Roughly speaking, all three nation-based parties received an overwhelming majority of the votes from their ethnic bases.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How was the first democratic government in Bosnia-Herzegovina formed? Who wanted what and who got what in that joint government?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Since the main opponent of all these three nation-based parties were the communists, these three parties did not differ much in anything, the HDZ, SDA, and the SDS. So they decided to create a partnership between them, with the main objective of politically restoring the entire Bosnia-Herzegovina. And senior posts were divided between them. I know when I already became Speaker of the Assembly, the Serbian Democratic Party wanted to achieve an economic revival. It was my dream and it was our policy that Bosnia-Herzegovina should be Switzerland in the Balkans. And on our side, although I did not participate in the negotiations about the division of senior posts, I know that we were supposed to receive security ministries. We wanted the economy, finances, and some other areas that would help us achieve our goals. So we ended up with a parliament which was neutral, whereas executive branches got assigned to the other two parties, the Muslim representative became prime minister -- sorry, president of the Presidency; and the Croatian one became prime minister. In the events that followed, we realised it was a great shortcoming that we only got the post of Speaker of the parliament, but we realised that too late. And eventually it led to a deterioration of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Which part of this division of posts do you consider as a shortcoming, as a failure?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: I believe the greatest failure was that the Ministry of the Interior and similar departments were given to the Muslims, to the Muslim side. You have seen, Your Honours, how many intercepts there are, completely unauthorised. I could never have imagined that a Speaker of the Assembly would be kept under surveillance or wire-tapped. I couldn't imagine that they would keep tabs on us if we were not doing it to them. That was the beginning of a conspiracy that began very early on against the Serbian side. Another important department was Territorial Defence and the post of president of the Presidency, although he was primus inter pares, he practically acted as the president of the republic, not one among equals.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After the government was established, were there any changes in terms of the strategic orientation of the leading three parties?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: What was shocking at the very first parliament session was that the oath was at issue. Simply, I was the parliament Speaker and there was a president of committee where we decided about this, the Chamber of Citizens, where Professor Konjicija was trying throughout one whole day to harmonise the conditions because, conditionally speaking, the Muslims and the Croatians didn't want "Yugoslavia" to be mentioned anywhere in the oath. And eventually the Serbian Democratic Party wanted to avoid a rift at the first parliament session and it eased off, and some sort of compromise was achieved. I can't remember it, but I'm sure that it wasn't accepted in the form that it should have been and as it had been originally proposed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As for the text of the hymn, was it regulated by anything, the constitution or the law, and did we violate it -- text of the anthem, we changed the text of this oath once we changed it against the procedure?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: The insistence on the change of the formulation of the oath was completely unlawful, and, Your Honours, it can be most easily seen if you look at the video recording of this very long parliament session when we struggled to find joint solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What did it mean and how did it further develop the attitude of those parties towards a joint state?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: From that moment until the end of the functioning of the parliament before the war, there was continuously a coalition of two against one, so that to be a Speaker of the parliament from the ethnic community against which you had two others was very difficult. It was very difficult to stand this rift because each new parliament session was an attempt to impose the majority of votes on the Serbian MPs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After the distribution of positions in the central and peripheral organ, were you in a position as the parliament Speaker to monitor the implementation of inter-party agreements on appointments of people to positions which had been allocated to their respective parties?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Certainly so, not just I as the parliament Speaker, but any representative of the authorities, even the lowest ones in municipalities were faced with impossibility to implement the partnership agreement about the distribution of positions in Bosnia-Herzegovina from the highest level to the lowest one in entire Bosnia-Herzegovina. And I can tell you this from the point of view of the Serbian Democratic Party. You had the right to appoint your staff somewhere. There were continuous obstructions. And just to recall you can see there how many important telephone conversations there were in which it was continuously mentioned how our staff were being obstructed from appointing other staff. Those were personnel from the communist times who transformed as turncoats and they started serving their new masters again. So the SDA accepted them because they would discharge their duties and wouldn't allow such personnel to be removed even though a specific position belonged, according to the agreement, to the Serbian Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, could you speak a bit slower. Please bear in mind. Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what were the main subjects of discussion and the main duties in the parliament, especially taking into account what you just recently said, namely, that at every parliament session there were attempts to out-vote the Serbian people. What were the issues in which the Serbian people were out-voted and what was the most sensitive issue in the parliament life?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: By the end of January 1992, the position of the Muslim Party of Democratic Action and the Serbian side had harmonised their positions, namely, that both sides advocated Yugoslavia, were in favour of Yugoslavia. And if you look at the parliament session held in late January, the president of the Presidency who was involved in the talks between the presidents of the republics of the then-Yugoslavia presented his exposé and he said what we should all be advocating and what was the position of the Party of Democratic Action. The Party of Democratic Action, just like the Serbian Democratic Party then advocated the preservation of Yugoslavia and a rational, reasonable Federation. Mr. Izetbegovic was then applauded by everyone present. From my seat of the parliament Speaker, I could not see whether the HDZ, that is to say, the Croatian MPs, applauded him, but the maximum majority supported this, that the parliament should advocate and that Bosnia-Herzegovina should advocate this reasonable Federation. Only a month later, in the very same room, Mr. Izetbegovic, on behalf of the Muslim side, said that the previous time we had not properly understood him and that he believed that Bosnia-Herzegovina, or rather, that Yugoslavia, let's say, conditionally speaking, should be transformed and that Bosnia-Herzegovina should secede from Yugoslavia. And he then said something that was an astonishing statement, namely, that he would sacrifice peace in order to achieve a sovereign state of Bosnia-Herzegovina. But no one understood that in a tragic sense then because there were all kinds of statements going around at the time. There was no reaction of the MPs after that nor did I react because I thought that it was something said in order to make a presentation for his voters who would understand him in a specific way. But now from this point of view, as this happened a hundreds times later, it was very problematic actually. Later on, that was a constant topic that was on the parliament's agenda, namely, the destiny of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The Muslim and the Croatian sides were in favour of a sovereign Bosnia-Herzegovina. They were in favour of Bosnia-Herzegovina seceding from Yugoslavia in an unconstitutional way. And on the Serbian side, we advocated honouring the constitution and finding a compromise, so that each parliament session was a new stress for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And putting aside what you know today, did you receive any information or data at the time as to whether those words about sacrificing peace were followed by any practical, organisational moves?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: I did receive information that I did not believe, that the Patriotic League was being formed, that paramilitary formations were being established, but as an idealist I believed that this was a matter of exaggerations because, honestly speaking, I did not trust the security people. But later on, reading documents, I could see that precisely at the time when Mr. Izetbegovic stated this, in the book of Mr. Sefer Halilovic, who was at that time the commander of their paramilitary formation, said that at the time he briefed Mr. Izetbegovic and said that he had 200.000 soldiers under arms. And then

utterances.speaker: MR. IZETBEGOVIC SAID
utterances.text: No problems. Now I can talk with the Serbian side on an equal footing. Someone had tricked Mr. Izetbegovic into changing his position, and I think that those who tricked him are more to blame than Mr. Izetbegovic himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us whether you and, according to what you knew, whether I also believed that this was really Mr. Izetbegovic's position. Initially you just said that someone pushed him or forced him to change his policy.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karadzic, you had a different role than me. You were a leader of a party which participated in the power. You were a leader of one ethnic group or people, and each time you were reserved and you warned that there could be a transformation, a big change, because it was your duty to warn in this way. Many information that I received, you received too, and you looked at that as the president of the party which had a duty to warn the people against what could happen. And eventually it turned out to be correct later on, so I wasn't right, but we played two different roles. And I understand the role of a leader who had to say something that he wouldn't like to believe would happen, simply as a politician. Everything seemed to point that the SDA policy would change. I still believed that it wouldn't happen, and that was why until the very beginning of the war I remained in the parliament as the Speaker.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did it turn out that the information that you received with regard to practical preparations for the war that you didn't believe turned out to be true?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Unfortunately, it turned out to be completely true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please show in e-court 1D49021.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, can you remind us, please, from which book does this page 95 come?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: I've read this book. It's the book of -- the memoirs of Mr. Alija Izetbegovic. I remember this article because during the preparation for my testimony I think I proposed this article as evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. May I then ask you to read out for us the second paragraph about two brave moves, the second and the third paragraphs out aloud, please.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: "However, during the summer," I apologise. "However, during the summer of 1991 we made two brave moves. Firstly, the SDA formed the National Defence Council, from which the Patriotic League would later be formed, and from it, during further development, the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That was on the 10th June 1991, after a rally in the local police centre which was attended by around 400 representatives from all of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The Yugoslav army was aware of this rally, but it did not react to it, it did not feel strong enough to react. Later on, in talks with the head of the counter-intelligence service in March 1992, I learned that they were aware of this. "The other move was our decision not to send the conscripts from Bosnia-Herzegovina to the JNA. That was in 1991 when the war in Croatia was in full swing. When I heard the disturbing news that General Nikola Uzelac, the commander of the army corps in Banja Luka, mobilised our young men and sent them to the front, I requested from the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina to make the decision that our young men should not respond to the call-ups for mobilisation. This decision was adopted by a majority of votes (the Serbian members of the Presidency voted against it)."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you then tell us whether you concluded that Mr. Izetbegovic himself was aware that this bravery had to do with the unlawful and illegal nature of these moves?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: That's completely true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Even though he mentions the 10th of June, 1991, as the date when the Muslims National Defence Council was established, did you learn since when are the years of service counted for the service in the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina or membership in the Patriotic League?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: The document exists. I cannot be very precise, but I know that it dates from March or April 1991 or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would ask for this page to be admitted into evidence and we will also attach the title page of the book. Just to be MFI'd until we receive the translation into English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't have any objection, Mr. President, but let me just note, I was slow to get on my feet, that -- just a caution about leading questions such as: "Can you tell us whether you concluded that ..." And then Dr. Karadzic provided an answer to which the witness agreed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Karadzic must have noted it. We'll mark it for identification, this excerpt, together with its cover page.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document receives MFI number D3996, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What were our intentions with regard to the duties of the parliament? What was the parliament supposed to deal with as its priorities and what did it actually do in fact, in real life, during those first months of 1991, or rather, throughout that year?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: The Serbian side wanted a democratic transformation of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the introduction of a multi-party system. The economic situation that existed at the time should be changed as soon as possible because there was social unrest, a difficult situation, and a war-mongering atmosphere which slowed down the normal course of life. Of course, the Serbian side also wanted for Serbian personnel to participate in power and to assist with improving and changing certain things that were wrong during the communist period, especially that the areas of Bosnia-Herzegovina that were rural and economically backward where Serbs lived should be protected in a way and to begin to develop and prosper once again. However, from the very beginning, the parliament, and up until the end of its one-and-a-half-year mandate, only dealt with one problem, and that was the future of Bosnia-Herzegovina; that is to say, whether Bosnia-Herzegovina should secede in an unconstitutional manner or should it remain in Yugoslavia and in what way would the political crisis in Bosnia-Herzegovina be resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us what you mean when you say "in an unconstitutional way"? What about the question of secession? How is it regulated in the constitution of Yugoslavia and the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Both in the constitution of Yugoslavia and in the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina, it was exactly spelled out how the republics, or rather, the peoples could separate from Yugoslavia and how that could be prevented from happening. The constitution of Yugoslavia had to be respected and the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In order to protect the peoples - and there were three main ethnic communities, the Serb, Croat, and Muslim communities - then a council for the equality of nations, or something like that, was established and everyone could lodge a complaint with that council. That could be discussed and then that question could be resolved with a two-third majority, only in that way, in that council, and in parliament. That is what had to be observed and that is what the Serbian side insisted upon. Also, two-thirds of the voters were not in favour of secession from Yugoslavia, so the other two sides insisted on somehow avoiding the council for national equality of rights because this was an unconstitutional path. That we were right is demonstrated by the current situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina. There is this Chamber of Citizens, if I can put it that way, and Chamber of Nations, and each constituent people had the right of "veto," I say that under quotation marks, if they disagree with a particular matter that threatened the national equality of rights of the three peoples.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us whether you were aware of the constitutional provisions and who the president of the constitutional commission of Bosnia-Herzegovina was?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: According to the rules of procedure and according to the practice that prevailed until then, the president of the parliament, that is to say, I, was the president of the constitutional commission. And therefore, we had to look into all the unconstitutional ways that were being resorted to to resolve that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said a moment ago that in parliament they did not have a two-third majority. What about the Serb side, especially the Serb Democratic Party, and other parties, too, that opposed secession, how many members of parliament did they have in the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina out of a total of 240?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: 240 MPs all together in the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina. As for the Assembly of Republika Srpska, 84 separated from that Assembly. So the Serb side had one-third that could dispute anything that was unconstitutional.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We saw here that on the 10th of June, a council for defending Muslims was established. Could you tell us how this affected parliamentary life in Bosnia-Herzegovina, life in general as well, or rather, the decisions of Slovenia and Croatia on secession, how did that affect life in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: As soon as secession happened, this automatically spilled over into Bosnia-Herzegovina and that was a very bad thing for peace in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Some people felt insecure, others felt buoyed by it, felt that they could take the same path like Slovenia and Croatia. The Serbs were worried, and the Muslims and Croats wanted to follow the road taken by Slovenia and Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about the first attempt in -- made in the Assembly to adopt a declaration on sovereignty? When was this attempt made and how did it fare?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: At the beginning of 1992 -- no, sorry, 1991, after Mr. Izetbegovic's statement that he would sacrifice peace for a sovereign Bosnia-Herzegovina, there was this proposal to adopt the declaration on sovereignty. It came from the Croatian side, as far as I can remember, and it was supported by the Muslim side, and then there was this lengthy debate where arguments for and against were confronted. And finally, according to strict procedure, 20 Serb MPs lodged a complaint - and this was a type of veto - and they invoked the council on the equality of rights of nations. And it was my duty then to conclude the debate and to refer the matter to the council for national equality. Since the sponsors of the bill reacted violently, then I called Avdo Campara, the late Avdo Campara, a Muslim, he spoke and explained this and he said President Krajisnik has the right to do that. That ended the debate. The council then dealt with the issue. We could not agree at the council because they did not want to honour the decision of the council and, quite simply, because the Muslim side opposed that and the Croat side, that question never came back to the Assembly, but procedurally that was necessary, that was a procedural obligation. It was supposed to be sent back to us so that we could express our views in the Assembly and in the council. So this proposal, this declaration, had it got a two-third majority, then it would have been valid. Of course, the Serb side would have had the right to refer the matter to the constitutional court, but these activities never took place because, quite simply, the Muslim side and the Croat side never wanted to go through the constitutional procedure that is envisaged in such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know what the reaction of the Serb side was in terms of their political moves, what were the political moves made and what were the activities of the Serb side in relation to developments in political life and the efforts made by the other two sides?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry. I was following the question until it broadened out so enormously. If we're still talking about this time-period in early 1991 and that's what Dr. Karadzic is soliciting information about, fair enough. But if this is as broad as he may perhaps inadvertently made it, it needs to be narrowed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The end of June 1991, we're still in that period. You have kindly presented the main topics involved and the main contentious issues. Tell us what the main moves of the Serb side were in Bosnia-Herzegovina up until the end of June 1991. You told us about the Assembly, but basically, on the ground, you said that they opposed secession.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: The Serb side, and that can be seen from documents, or rather, the leaders or people who held high office in the municipalities and also coming from you directly, the Serb side always appealed for pacification and not to go into conflicts on the ground. People were worried on the ground, there were different reactions, especially after a statement that was made in haste, if you will, by Mr. Izetbegovic. When the declaration was refused, then after the agreement reached between and among the presidents of the republics of Yugoslavia he said in Split: The declaration would be adopted with the Serbs or without the Serbs, it's all the same. There was a tempestuous reaction on the ground; people were alarmed. Paramilitary formations appeared. People were saying that the Muslims were preparing an attack on the Serb Krajina and that they would attack Bosnia and Herzegovina. You will see from the documents - and I remember this - many appeals made by the Main Board and by the president of the party to have the situation calm down and at that time an initiative was launched. I can't remember whether it was the MBO, the Muslim Bosniak Organisation, or whether it was Mr. Karadzic directly, to reach a historical agreement between the Muslims and the Croats, because these two peoples had a lot more in common than the Croats with the other two peoples. So then these activities started with regard to the historical agreement. Then there was a relaxation of tensions. The newspapers and TV stations were reacting to this favourably. People were trying to accommodate each other because they really did want to have pacification. During these activities, I had two meetings at Mr. Izetbegovic's office. He was not in charge of that action and it wasn't the SDA, and then there was one meeting in my office. So I know that this was a major positive turn and most of the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina reacted to that favourably, irrespective of the ethnic community they belonged to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We will go back to that. I would like to ask you to tell us -- you said that there were pressures on the ground. Did the Serb side do anything? And if you remember the community of municipalities, could you please first explain that to us. Were there communities of municipalities? How were they regulated? And how and in which way could they be changed, the composition of the communities of municipalities?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Communities of municipalities are a constitutional possibility of bringing together municipalities in Bosnia-Herzegovina. That existed before the war, in the communist times, and since we still had that constitution in force, then municipalities could be joined in a perfectly lawful manner. Several municipalities could unite several functions at the level of a community of municipalities. It wasn't only economic, although it was primarily economic, economic requirements, if you will, because in communism, in the former system, nobody thought about war or anything like that or uniting on a national or ethnic level. So it was economic parameters that were of primary importance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How did you understand the question of the establishment of regions? What was the reason for the regions to be established? In the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina, what was adopted as a document in relation to these regions?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: At the time, unfortunately, everything in Bosnia-Herzegovina was politics because everybody was disturbed, old men, old women, children, women, everybody, this spectacle of our disagreement was all over the place. However, the regions were established because traditionally certain areas had been neglected in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Unfortunately, since the Serbs had most of the territory, it was these Serb territories that were neglected the most. We were aware of that problem, and in the former system there was this antagonism between Banja Luka and Sarajevo, there was this antagonism or objections because many ethnic Serb areas were basically being emptied. So what we wanted was to have this programme, if everything would be normal and nobody gave a thought to war, to have balanced development in Bosnia-Herzegovina. In this balanced development, communities and municipalities would play an important role. So that was the initial reason. Economic links was the first reason, and secondly, this was possible on the basis of the constitution and everything that was derived from all of that and that perhaps assumed a different connotation later, all of that was a result of efforts made to impose solutions on the Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the Serb side prepared to do and sacrifice? Do you remember what a concession was on the Serb side in favour of the historic Serb/Muslim agreement? What did the Muslims want in return in order to have this Muslim/Serb agreement come into being?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: The Muslim/Bosniak organisation - it's a smaller political party and these are high-level intellectuals - they wanted to avoid war at all costs just like the Serb side, so then there was this compromise. Bosnia-Herzegovina would remain in Yugoslavia, and automatically the Serb side would give up on regionalisation which made others a bit apprehensive. So our maximum concession was to have a decentralisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but that there should be nothing that would resemble Serb homogenisation. So the concession was for Bosnia-Herzegovina to remain in Yugoslavia but to be a reasonable federation -- a reasonable federation -- rather, Yugoslavia should be a reasonable federation and there should be maximum privileges for Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the Serb side would not ask for any kind of regionalisation that would have any kind of political overtones.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said a moment ago that it was welcomed with relief or delight - I cannot remember what you said exactly. Could you tell us what the reactions were of the Muslim and the Serb sides to this?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: If you look at the TV footage from the time, and I will remind you of what I know, all citizens could see that on the spot, on the ground, and on television and over the radio too, in companies, in municipalities, there was general delight, celebration, because everybody wanted that to happen, all citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The Party of Democratic Action, when did they withdraw support to that initiative and how was it experienced at that point of view and how did things develop further?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: I know that, and this was best described by one of the then-participants, Professor Muhamed Filipovic, who said that Mr. Zulfikarpasic and Professor Nikola Koljevic, I think, appeared on television to declare that this historic agreement had been reached. And during the TV programme itself, somebody said to Mr. Zulfikarpasic to come out, and then he was told that the Party of Democratic Action did not support that and that this was a private affair of Mr. Zulfikarpasic's and Mr. Radovan Karadzic's, which was completely incorrect because I took part in these talks at Mr. Izetbegovic's office and he supported that, he gave it a green light, as I did, to continue negotiations and to have this agreement reached.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I beg the indulgence of the Prosecution because I did not announce this material, but I should like to put on the ELMO this statement made by Mr. Izetbegovic in Split. First, the front page, to see the date, and then the rest of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting, Mr. President, did the Assembly impose a ban or adopt another measure concerning these regions?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: I remember the talks that preceded this enactment by the government, because it was the government that made the decision, and the prime minister, Mr. Pelivan, came to see me with his deputy, Mr. Cengic, and in the talks, they told me they will not impose a ban but they will make a recommendation to defuse the tensions. So the government proposed that the establishment of regions be put on hold until the spirits calm down. So they did not say no to the regions, but since the political situation was getting more complicated, it was put on hold, and of course, the effect achieved by this government measure was soon invalidated.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do we have any problems with the ELMO? Can we switch it on? [In English] So please show the first page to see the date --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think the ELMO is working at the moment. Yes, it's now working. It's up to you, Mr. Karadzic, how to use your time, but are you not spending too much time on this historical background? Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, that's year 1991. This is not the historical background. This is the peak of the events, preparation for war. [In English] First page, please. Yeah, okay, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, can you tell us what is the date and what is the newspaper?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: It's newspaper "Politika," as far as I can see 30th March 1991, a Saturday.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What is the heading about? It's a report from where?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: It's a report from Split. The heading is: Press conference held by the presidents of the six Yugoslav republics. And the subheading is: Great difference but also -- great differences but also a desire to bridge them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Right corner of the second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I ask you to read out Izetbegovic's statement.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: That's okay. That's okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that's precisely the statement I referred to a moment ago. Alija Izetbegovic says: "I will immediately answer the second question. The declaration on sovereignty is already before the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina and will most probably be endorsed. If it is not endorsed with the consent of the SDS, it will be endorsed without them. At the end of the day, Bosnia-Herzegovina is a sovereign republic and the declaration is just one document. Bosnia does not become sovereign by the virtue of this document. It is a declaration of an already-existing fact."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic needs to wait for the interpretation to finish before starting his new question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You overlapped with the interpretation. Could you repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were they able to adopt this declaration without the consent of the SDS in terms of the constituent position of the Serbian people and also in terms of the two-third majority rule?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: They could not adopt this without the participation of the Serbian representatives in the parliament, either in theory or in practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could both pages please be admitted into evidence pending the translation of this statement? Or if you believe that what we have on the record is sufficient ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are you tendering it or not?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I am tendering, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Obviously I'm not quite sure what else is on those pages, but barring -- and what else is proposed to be translated, but -- which I presume is the entirety of what he's tendering, though, the page on which the question and the answer appear and the cover page of the document, then I have no objection particularly to those.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: But, it will be MFI'd, and as is the case with all of these things, given its - as Dr. Karadzic noted - his late notice and the fact that our ability to examine on this is obviously limited, I will obviously reserve any further comment on this until we see the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark those parts referred to by Mr. Karadzic for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It receives MFI number D3997, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, can you remember, what was the reaction of Serbian authorities at the grass-root level to this cancellation of the historical -- the historic, rather, Serbian/Muslim agreement, especially in the Krajina of Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: The reaction was fierce. And the leadership of the Serbian Democratic Party had huge problems because urgent action was needed to unify the two Krajinas, the Serbian and the Bosnian Krajina, and there were major objections voiced to the leadership of the SDS, that their policies were not realistic because the other side does not wish for peace.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember when and on what occasion the association of municipalities from the Banja Luka region was proclaimed as the Autonomous Region of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: I don't know when it was proclaimed exactly, but I know that it was only towards the end of the year that we finally verified or approved the creation of the regions, including that one, because new political factors had cropped up by that time. It was quite clear that there was no consensus, the declaration was passed by a majority vote, and the request for international recognition was submitted to the European community. So I think it was on the 10th of December that the regions were approved, but even then it was said that if the request for unilateral recognition is not taken back, we would come back to the historic principles, whereby Bosnia and Herzegovina remains within Yugoslavia and the Serbian side would not continue the course towards political regionalisation although it would continue with economic regionalisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, D3997, that "Politika" article we looked at, is already in evidence as D00258.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. And thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If it is confirmed by the Defence, we'll strike out the marked for identified part, but shall we continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Concerning the failure of the historic Muslim/Serbian agreement and the tensions on the ground, what did the Assembly that you presided over do in early September?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Since the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina was being tested to the limit, there were talks within the Assembly. And then in early September, Mr. Izetbegovic proposed the conclusion at one of the sessions that the future arrangement for Bosnia and Herzegovina be decided by taking into account all proposals at an equal footing without imposing anything on the others and that the final solution for Bosnia and Herzegovina should be found in a democratic and constitutional way. And I believe he proposed that conclusion on the 13th or 14th of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you said proposals should be considered on an equal footing, what did that imply?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Maybe I misinterpreted it, but I meant to say that all proposals for the solution for Bosnia and Herzegovina should be treated equally. We already knew from our talks that we disagree on many things, even every political party had its own vision for Bosnia and Herzegovina. So the idea was that all MPs present their proposals in parliamentary debates, that they all be debated democratically, and that a solution be found after considering all these proposals and after all these debates in keeping with democratic principles and the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember when the first ideas appeared about the transformation of Bosnia along ethnic lines, based on its ethnic structure, and who voiced these ideas first?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Since we were constantly in contact with representatives of the other two sides, I myself in the Assembly and others in their departments, I heard from Mr. Izetbegovic and others that the best solution would be to divide Bosnia-Herzegovina. However, Bosnia-Herzegovina is a leopard skin when you see it on an ethnic map. So it should be done by creating three parts in which as few Croats would remain in the Serb and Muslim parts, as few Serbs in the Croat and Muslim parts, et cetera. And Izetbegovic said: Let's try to make a map wherein as few of us would be on your side and as few of you as possible on our side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue. Please try to put a pause as much as possible.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How did late Mr. Izetbegovic view the possibility of establishing a Serb entity and the possibility that the Serb entity would remain within Yugoslavia and become independent?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: As you can see from his own book and the book of Mr. Sefer Halilovic and the book of Muhamed Filipovic, Mr. Izetbegovic was always in favour of creating a new Bosnia and Herzegovina, transformed, where nobody would impose solutions on others. That was in the early days, because he was a pragmatic politician. If you look at his book, you will see that he says: Late Arafat made this suggestion to me and I fought over this with Sefer Halilovic, and a few years later I described one declaration where he proposed, and Owen and Stoltenberg supported it, proposing that the future Republika Srpska would have the option of organising a referendum within five years to join Serbia. I remember one discussion in 1993, in Geneva, where Izetbegovic and Silajdzic came to see us and said: Give us 33 per cent of Bosnia. Let us create three entities and then you are free to go and join Serbia. This entire policy was conducted, and you will see, Your Honours, the transcripts of the parliament of Bosnia and Herzegovina, they were thinking about dividing Bosnia and Herzegovina in such a way that each nation would have its sovereignty. That was the policy. I'm not defending Mr. Izetbegovic, but I believe that that was his sincere, honest, policy. However, he had too many people around him who had this idea affixed that Bosnia should be unitarian, that, if necessary, it should be achieved by war, et cetera. And that is the problem. His early idea expressed in the declaration and many other documents and proposals was travestied.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Excellencies, I see the time. If you decide for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll have a break for half an hour and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, to save time the Chamber is of the view that it is able to give its ruling without hearing the parties any more about the interviews of Mr. Kovac. Would you like to --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I was going to say that we -- Mr. Nicholls, of course, was duly suited up and prepared to come down, but it appeared to us that if we met with Mr. Robinson at the lunch break, we might be able to narrow the range of disagreement, and thereby reduce the number of issues the Court needed to deal with. But if the Court has already made its -- taken its position, there's not much I can say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber was of the view that it tended to agree with Mr. Robinson's observation that those parts that were fully read out and those parts the witness didn't answer are not to be -- were not to be admitted. And -- but if the parties are minded to have further discussion --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- the Chamber has no observation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks. I guess the discussion was, yes, to the extent we may -- we may -- that the -- that there is agreement that where a passage is fully read out and the witness affirms it, the practice has been - and we agree with that - then the documentation is superfluous because the witness has adopted it. On the other hand, where the witness disputes it, then it serves as impeachment; or, alternatively, where the passage is merely paraphrased, then the entirety of the impeachment should come in. Now, whether or not the application of those principles will lead to full agreement by the parties, I won't know until the lunch break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think that can be dealt with after Mr. Karadzic's examination-in-chief is over. So I would like to hear from the parties at that time. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. With respect to Exhibit D3997, we appreciate the Prosecution bringing to our attention that it was admitted under D259. However, the English version doesn't include the comments by Mr. Izetbegovic, and so if we could submit that for translation and add it to D259, that would be okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll do so. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How did these conclusions of the joint Assembly, from the first week or the first third of September 1991, about not imposing a solution accepted by the public and how long did this obligation last, namely, that nothing would be imposed?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Just like in any similar situation, the people relaxed. The tensions subsided and a general positive feeling reigned. Unfortunately, after only a month another shock followed and a very problematic item was on the agenda, once again a declaration in some other form, and then a rift took place in the parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please briefly tell the Chamber what was put on the agenda, how did the session progress in its regular part, and then afterwards to the end?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: On the 10th of October, and then up until the 14th, practically every day the session was in progress or between the sessions, various meetings were held in order to resolve the repeated attempt of the Muslim side to put the declaration on the sovereignty of Bosnia-Herzegovina in an unconstitutional way on the agenda in a different form. In these periods between sessions, the positions got closer together in various ways, solutions were adopted, compromises were made, but eventually the situation became the same as it had been in March that same year, that is to say, 1991. After a long and exhausting discussion - and it was exactly the same as when the declaration was rejected - the Serbian deputies from the Serbian Democratic Party and Serbian Renewal Movement once again submitted a request with 20 signatures that this item of the agenda should be delegated to the council for inter-ethnic equality. And then I ended the session. The procedure was the same; however, when I declared that the session was finished and when we left, I actually said that we were going on a break and the session was scheduled for the next Monday and also in hope that there would be certain improvements after that. According to the constitution, the session could not continue in any way after that, but the Muslim/Croatian coalition which had already been in existence waited ten minutes and, contrary to the constitution, the deputy Speaker, who did not have the same powers as myself, continued the session. They adopted the conclusions, a resolution, adopted the documents which now had a different title but they were identical to the declaration for which we had once concluded that it was contrary to the constitution and that it should be dealt with by the inter-ethnic equality council.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Here in the indictment and in some documents as well, it is stated that the Serbian deputies left or walked out of the session and the Assembly, depending on the document. Did the Serbian deputies leave the joint Assembly or the session?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: No, they didn't leave it or walk out. I ended the session and after that it could not have been continued.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And did the Serbian deputies leave the joint Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: No, they did not join -- they did not leave the joint Assembly or walk out of it. What followed was an invitation, I even scheduled the continuation of the session, but none of the other sides responded to that. Then certain political activities began, the invitations of the Serbian side to rescind the unconstitutional decisions which they believed to be valid and the Serbian side didn't. We wanted to bring our positions closer to one another in order to resolve this difficult political issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the next move of the Serbian side after these invitations that the unconstitutional decisions be withdrawn?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: As far as I remember, it was on the 17th or on the 19th of October. The Serbian side sent a public invitation, both to the population and to the other sides, to rescind the decisions, and unless they were rescinded, the Serbian side would then pass a decision on proclaiming the Assembly of the Serbian People in Bosnia-Herzegovina which would be a substitute for the inter-ethnic equality council which had not been established because we couldn't find a satisfactory solution together with the Muslim and Croatian sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the following move of the Serbian side, the Serbian deputies?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: On the 24th -- I apologise. On the 24th of October, the Serbian side proposed or called on the ethnic Serbian deputies from the Assembly. That was actually a general initiative, and the Assembly of the Serbian People in Bosnia-Herzegovina was established.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you talked about the conclusions from the 19th of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The 11th of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: -- 1991 that they would not be imposed on anyone, I would like to recall that it was an excerpt from the Official Gazette of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It's already an Exhibit, D265. The conclusions which eased off the political situation are quoted there. Thank you. Mr. President, can you tell us if by establishing their Assembly, which as you said had the importance of the chamber of nationalities which was missing by that time, did the Serbian deputies leave their deputies' places in the Assembly or did they continue to work?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: They did not leave their places. They did not cease to be members of the parliament, but they in a way froze their participation. At the proposal of all the deputies, I myself continued to discharge my duty as the parliament Speaker in the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina in order to seek a political solution and in order to overcome the crisis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us what was the next move of the Serbian Assembly -- actually, the Assembly of the Serbian People in terms of collecting the opinions and views of the entire Serbian community?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: After the attacks in the media to the effect that one political party, the Serbian Democratic Party, was articulating its own policy rather than the will of all of the Serbian people, the decision was made at the session when we established the council of the Serbian people, the Assembly of the Serbian people, to organise a plebiscite where all the Serbian people could vote because we wanted to have an expression of the will of the Serbian people about this issue, the issue of the future of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It was said here that we made it possible for Croats and Muslims and everyone else to state their mind, but specifically on a yellow piece of paper. The suggestion was that we had racially discriminatory attitude toward them. Can you remember how this progressed and why these specific papers were of yellow colour?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: The goal and the duty which followed from the objections of the other side was to establish the will of the Serbian people, because the Serbian people, their representatives, had the right to send a question to the council for inter-ethnic equality. And because it wasn't done, then the objection was that this was not the will of the people but the will of the party which was represented in the parliament. So the goal was to establish the will of one people and we had to know how many Serbs were in favour or what was their opinion about this issue, and then it was made possible to the others to do it too because it's not true that only Serbs were in favour of Yugoslavia. There were pro-Yugoslav parties seated in Sarajevo which also wanted to have Yugoslavia preserved and protected the interests of Bosnia and Herzegovina in their own way, but that was almost identical to the way that the Serbian Democratic Party was doing it. That was why there were different voting papers without any discriminatory intention. In particular, we tried to make sure that no one would object and compare that to what was happening in World War II, when the Jews, the Serbs, and the Romas were maltreated and discriminated in our part of the world. So it is completely excluded, this possibility of interpreting it as a wish to discriminate someone. It was just in order to determine how many people from which ethnic group voted. I don't actually remember which colours were used, but I know that we did take that into account and our commission emphasised that in its report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the situation like in Croatia at the time?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Beyond the borders of Bosnia-Herzegovina, towards Croatia and the west, the war was in full swing so that every minor incident in this area was reflected on the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. From the position you were in, did you have any insight into the situation with regard to the arming of the ethnic groups in Bosnia-Herzegovina? Did you have any information about this, and what was the impact of the war in Croatia on Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Yes. Very frequently we received various information. There is a well-known incident with illegal arming via Hungary. I think that the minister of the interior of Yugoslavia was the one who organised it at the time, and I believe that that was Martin Spegelj. That was known to everyone. We had other information too to the effect that Croatia and Slovenia were arming themselves, and also individual reports, both official and unofficial, that the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina were also being armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know, did you receive any information, how far the Patriotic League was developed in terms of organisation and obtaining weapons, their military organisation, I mean both the Green Berets and the Patriotic League. At that moment in mid-October, what did you know about the arming of the Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: There was a lot of information, least of all official, but through various channels there were these reports that paramilitary formations were being formed among the Muslims, in the Muslim community. And as for the Croats, certain things were happening, in particular in western Herzegovina, where the paramilitary formations or perhaps even lawful formations from Croatia, I mean formations belonging to the Croatian state, were present in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So there was a continuous flow of this information that we received to the effect that the preparations for war and for arming were ongoing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What were the following moves of the Croatian/Muslim part of the authorities and what were the moves of the Serbian side; that is to say, when was the next parliament session of the Serbian Assembly held and what were the measures or the counter-measures that were taken at the time?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: The session on the 24th of October. Our session when we established the Assembly of the Serbian people did not much concern the Muslim side. They continued going along their own way, and we kept receiving information that their aspiration was to have Bosnia-Herzegovina secede by force and, contrary to the constitution, from Yugoslavia. In addition to the invitations to begin negotiations which were never accepted, on the 22nd there was another session of the Serbian Assembly, and then the next one on the 21st of December. Namely, it was clear that our partners didn't want to have constitutionality back in Bosnia-Herzegovina. They wanted to continue doing what they did previously, which was unconstitutional. So that on several occasions we insisted on re-establishing constitutionality, on having negotiations, and when that yielded no fruit and it didn't -- because the then-European community called on Bosnia-Herzegovina and other former Yugoslav republics to ask for their independence to be recognised. When that happened, the government which was not authorised to do this and the Presidency which was not authorised to do this, by out-voting the Serbian members of the Presidency, adopted the conclusion to send this request for the recognition of the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. When that happened, I think it was on the 15th of December, we scheduled a session for the 21st of December, at which we clearly said: Unless you rescind these unlawful decisions and unless you withdraw the request that the independence be recognised, then the Serbian people and the Serbian deputies will pass a decision on the proclamation of the republic of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And namely, in the meantime there were meetings with a number of representatives of the international community where we were clearly told that negotiations would follow, that we would discuss the future of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that if we accepted this international recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina that we would be entitled to having our constitutive unit within Bosnia-Herzegovina. I did not participate in negotiations with international representatives. These were Mr. Vance, Mr. Carrington, and others also came. You were the one who talked with them at the time, Mr. President, and so did the Deputy President, Mr. Koljevic, and I know that this was something that you were the first to learn. And then I learned that we would have our constitutive unit, an ethnic one. I received this information around the New Year's Day at a meeting that was held at the invitation of the late Slobodan Milosevic in Belgrade. Wherever -- whatever we heard directly later on from Mr. Cutileiro, we heard then first from him. Our proposal is that you should accept independent and internationally recognised Bosnia and that you would get your ethnic unit within Bosnia, and our policy was corrected a bit in a way. Publicly we had to stick to our view that we wanted to remain in Yugoslavia, but we accepted and later on confirmed this in the Assembly that we would accept Bosnia-Herzegovina but we wanted to have our own entity within it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you react to the decisions of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Muslim/Croat part of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, you as president of the Assembly, when they asked for independence? Do you remember, did you communicate with anyone in that period of time?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I wrote a letter and I sent it to the representatives of the international community, as far as I can remember, that is. The Assembly did react, that is correct, and I on behalf of the Assembly informed the international community, the European community, that the decisions of the Presidency and the government were unconstitutional and that they should bear in mind that there is a special situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that it's not a sort of normal situation like in other republics of Bosnia-Herzegovina, because politically there are three different views and they have to be taken into account. And the proposal that they are receiving, namely, to recognise the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is not in accordance with the constitution and it goes against the will of the Serb people who have the right to challenge that kind of decision because it's unconstitutional.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
