utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, asking the other side for their understanding, 1D02136, could that document be shown to the witness. And again, I'm sorry that I haven't notified the other side of that. There is no Serbian version, so could we please blow up the English version?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what the document is and could you tell us what it says in the heading.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: That's correct. This is a document that I signed, although my signature is not there. I remember that. This is the Assembly of the Serb People in Bosnia-Herzegovina on the 22nd of December. That is to say, a day after this session, this was sent to Lord Carrington and Henry Wijnaendts, Van den Broek, Christian Braun, then Mr. Janssen, the UN general-secretary, the UN Security Council, the embassies of 12 in Belgrade, the embassy of the USSR in Belgrade, the embassy of the USA in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please show us the last page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I believe that we can see your signature there.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: I believe it's only written in the English language. Somebody wrote that up and I signed it. That's right. This is my signature at the bottom of the page, and perhaps that is the first page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm going to read out part of first and second paragraph what it was you wrote to these respectable people. [As read][In English] "By illegal demand for independency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, you have once again drastically overthrown the constitutional and law order and endangered peace which relies only on goodwill and sense of our citizens. With this act you have violated taken oath and disqualified yourselves in front of the present and the history for further managing affairs of state why people placed trust in you but with completely different election programmes." [Interpretation] What did you mean by this?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Precisely what I said a moment ago. As far as I can remember, although I cannot see it here, this is a letter that is addressed to the Presidency of the Bosnia-Herzegovina and the others persons were CC'd, the persons I mentioned a moment ago. I said that -- actually, this was an illegal move, the one that they took, and in this way they betrayed, actually, the trust of the citizens who voted for them. And, in fact, they made a turn-around which seriously jeopardises peace. And peace is actually being maintained just through the goodwill of citizens not through a wise policy conducted by politicians.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us whether you remember Badinter's reaction? Perhaps he didn't write to you directly, but how did he react in the recommendations for Bosnia-Herzegovina? Why did Bosnia-Herzegovina not win his approval straight away? Rather, in opinion number 4, Badinter set some prerequisites.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: I think, as far as I can remember, maybe I'm wrong, I remember that Mr. Badinter did write to me and it was a similar letter and it can be found in the documents. A reaction did follow and it was stated that Bosnia-Herzegovina is not an ordinary state, if I can put it that way, and that there are certain specific characteristics involved, and that it is necessary to see the will of the citizens and that these special characteristics have to be borne in mind. That is the reason why, in this first stage, Bosnia-Herzegovina was not recognised; rather, time was given to carry out other activities so that these remarks could be checked in a way and so that a climate could be created that would make it possible for war to be avoided.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the participants, this opinion of Badinter that President Krajisnik is referring to is D1279. It has already been admitted, D1279. Thank you. Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I see the title of this page, the upper part of this page. This is a warning, to who? SR B. and H. Presidency. What is SR? Is it Socialist Republic or the Serbian Republic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Presidency and the government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. It's a compilation of several documents which was sent to the Secretary-General and Mr. Carrington?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Yes, Excellency. [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Krajisnik is indicating the basis on which he is writing to them, and then he CC'd the others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. President, I didn't have an objection, but you mentioned the word "compilation," maybe I missed that. I'm just seeing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you see first page is the cover page, second page is a letter to the SG of the United Nations, and third page is a letter sent to Carrington which contains several documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't have any objection in principle. I'd like to look at the specific documents. But let's -- I'll raise -- if I encounter anything that is worth raising, I will raise it quickly; otherwise, no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll admit it. Shall we use the previous number? Exhibit D3997.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did I hear this wrong or did you skip the session of the Assembly of the Serb People that was held on the 11th of December? It is important for me because of a particular document. Before the 21st of December, was another session of the Serb people held on the 11th of December?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: That's correct. On the 11th of December, a session of the Assembly was held and I did not mention it a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that a recommendation was adopted then to the effect that where conditions are right Serb municipalities should be established?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: That is correct. On the 11th of December a decision was passed. But there's just a small correction there. To establish Serb Municipal Assemblies, that is to say, bodies like the Assembly of the Serb People.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I do apologise. So not municipalities but Assemblies of municipalities, parliaments, Serb parliaments in these municipalities; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was this obligatory, mandatory, or was this a recommendation; namely, that if they felt the need to do so, they could establish that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: The stenographic notes readily show that after a long debate, yielding to pressure coming from people from the grass roots, this recommendation was adopted, because we thought that this Assembly that we established at the level of Bosnia-Herzegovina at one point in time would simply cease to exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In which conditions would these Assemblies, these Serb parliaments at central level and at local levels, cease to exist? What would have to happen for them to cease to exist?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: The first requirement was to go back to constitutionality and to discuss the future set-up in Bosnia-Herzegovina on a constitutional basis. Once that would happen, the decision on the establishment of the Assembly of the Serb People in Bosnia-Herzegovina would no longer be in force as well as these Municipal Assemblies; and their task was just to intervene at first, just to intervene at that moment when the constitution would be violated to the detriment of the Serb people at any level.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D1183, could we please have that in e-court. In English we first have the preamble and then the rest is probably on the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see the upper right-hand corner, is that that recommendation?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Yes, that is that recommendation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Next page in English, please. [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, here in the indictment there is a reference to a certain paper that is called Variant A and Variant B here. Are you aware of the existence of such a paper and how does this paper relate to this recommendation to establish municipalities?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: As for Variants A and B, I testified in my own trial so everything I'm going to say now is contained there. There was no need to pass this document that was called Variant A and B if we had this recommendation that was adopted earlier on. There is no causal relationship between the recommendation and the subsequently adopted paper entitled: "Variant A and B." So on the basis of this recommendation, every municipality, every group of Assemblymen could establish a municipality, a Municipal Assembly, a parliament, and satisfy the things contained in Variants A and B. I stated that in my own testimony - you can find it there. I did not know when it was distributed, this document. Allegedly it was distributed during one session. Now was it a session of the Main Board or a session of the Assembly at the Holiday Inn, somebody could have distributed that just in passing, by the by, but it's not that I know that it was being distributed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As for this recommendation, was it discussed at the Assembly and was a decision passed?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: A moment ago I mentioned this. If you look at the stenographic notes from that session, you will see that the initiative came from some members of parliament at that session and there was a great deal of hesitation. We hesitated to make a decision. And then a compromise was reached to give a recommendation, that on the ground, on the spot, each and every municipal parliament, or rather, Serb MPs in municipalities could decide whether they felt that was necessary or not. Many did, many did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. President, what does the Assembly produce or what does a Assembly produce? And if an Assembly produces something, does it first have to be on the agenda? Does it have to be debated first before being adopted? Could you tell us what kind of documents are adopted by an Assembly and what has to be on the agenda in the debate and then in the conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: In the rules of procedure of the Assembly, it is obligatory to allocate time for presenting documents which would be included in the agenda. These documents are then discussed, conclusions are made, decisions are made. In fact, documents are passed which are within the purview of the Assembly, those are decisions, conclusions, laws, declarations, et cetera. And all these documents that are discussed and that must be presented in advance, all the conclusions made have to be promulgated in the Official Gazette of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The Assembly cannot pass anything without promulgating it. A moment ago you saw one of the conclusions. There were many conclusions, but conclusions were, in fact, groundwork for a different document. Once debate is concluded, a decision is made, et cetera. There was a conclusion of 11 September that was so important that it was promulgated in the Official Gazette too. Nothing can be passed by the Assembly without it being published in the Official Gazette, at least according to the law it shouldn't be. And because the rules of procedure prescribed that one had to announce in advance what would be discussed in the Assembly, the Party of Democratic Action once wanted to interrupt the session in order to include a new item in the agenda. I stopped it and the lawyers cautioned all of us that the Assembly may not work in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here we have some general documents from the Assembly admitted into evidence, transcripts and records of Assembly sessions. Can you tell us if there is any difference between transcripts and records, is there any essential difference?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: In the Serbian language, a transcript produced by shorthand is a kind of record produced by shorthand, and if something was missing the audiotape would be checked, whereas a record would include only the main points of the session. A record is not a verbatim reflection of the session, whereas the transcript shows exactly the course of the debate word for word.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can the record include something that was not adopted or vice versa?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Well, if that happens that can only be by human error, that somebody missed something. The record reflects the conclusions that were adopted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was the fate of some extreme or angry discussions that happened in the Assembly that we can see in transcripts but we cannot see them in the records? How did that happen?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: In records you will see almost no reflection of any discussions, just the conclusions, and that's important. Deliberations are very elaborate, very detailed, but the record will reflect only the end result, the conclusions. It's important for a journalist or anybody who wants to read about it, but for me and various services in the Assembly it's also important to have a correct record.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When we were talking about Serbian Assemblies in municipalities, that is to say, Serbian parliaments - and we will discuss it also later in connection with Serb territories - here in my case there is an adjudicated fact number 1932 which is that the SDS was prepared to separate Serbian territories from Bosnia-Herzegovina if that was the only way of keeping them within Yugoslavia. Is this true according to what you know? And did we stand firmly by our priority objective of staying within Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: As I stated previously, the Serbian side until the end of 1991 had a priority task of staying within Yugoslavia; however, we then had talks with various representatives, and I know from talking to Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Koljevic as well as with Mr. Vance and Lord Carrington and later Mr. Milosevic as well, we realised that if we wanted to pursue a realistic policy on a global level we had to work towards staying within Bosnia and Herzegovina even if we can't stay within Yugoslavia. So this conclusion is not correct. That territory was part of Yugoslavia at that time anyway, and all the way up until the time when the problem of Bosnia-Herzegovina is resolved, it would remain within Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Another adjudicated fact, 1946, claims that our Assembly of the Serbian People proclaimed its territory as the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in January 1991, including all the populated areas, municipalities, et cetera, which declared at the referendum that they wanted to stay as a part of Yugoslavia. Did we indeed have the intention to proclaim our territory a part of Yugoslavia and did we need anybody's approval or consent for that in November 1991?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: I don't know the exact wording of that, but the aim of the plebiscite was for the Serbian people to declare their will, whether they were for a united Bosnia-Herzegovina or for staying in Yugoslavia. So we obtained a map in which certain areas responded differently. There was no point for us in claiming that these areas are part of Yugoslavia, but we did want to show in which areas the Serbian people declared that they were for Yugoslavia. It was not our objective to say Yugoslavia is from here and up to here it's not. As long as the Bosnia-Herzegovina issue was open, that was not the case. But for the Serbian Democratic Party it was a basis for drawing maps later in negotiations when we were negotiating with the other side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If we're going to engage in this exercise, Mr. President, of purporting to recite the witness adjudicated facts and asking for his -- or trying to elicit a response from him on it, then two things need to occur. Number one, the adjudicated fact needs to be correctly recited. Here I see the question was: "Another adjudicated fact ... claims that our Assembly of the Serbian People proclaimed its territory as the territory ..." et cetera, et cetera. The adjudicated fact in fact states: "On November 21st, 1991, the Bosnian Serb Assembly proclaimed as part of the territory of federal Yugoslavia," et cetera. So if we start in the proposition that it's difficult to elicit a response of any assistance to the Court, and then secondly, there apparently was no interest on the part of Dr. Karadzic in actually eliciting an answer responsive to that question because the response seemed to address the plebiscite and other aspects rather than the terms of the adjudicated fact itself. I won't intervene in this way in future, but I will make a marker that such questions and answers have no impact on the adjudicated facts whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: One point, be precise in referring to the adjudicated facts. It's important to read out correctly. Shall we continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency. I wanted to save time, but as usual, I end up wasting more time in this way. I will leave aside the adjudicated facts until I obtain the correct citation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Speaker, after the 11th of December, which was the next session of the Assembly of the Serbian People of Bosnia and Herzegovina and what was the occasion?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: The date was 21st December, and the occasion was the unlawful request of the Muslim and Croat part of the Presidency and the Muslim/Croat government to apply for international recognition with the European community.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Two days before that, on the 19th of December, did you attend the plenary session of the Serbian Democratic Party?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You've already discussed this. Was there any debate about papers A and B, debate and decision?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If a session of a Municipal Assembly would include in its agenda those instructions or recommendations that were adopted at the meeting of the 21st December, would that be party instructions or Assembly instructions?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: I have to be precise. When I said it was not discussed at the plenary session, at the same time there was also a club of MPs of the Serbian Assembly, where I dealt with preparations for the 21st December session. So I did not really participate much in the plenary session. Could you clarify your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If in an agenda of a Municipal Assembly we read: "Consideration of the recommendations adopted by the Assembly of 21st December," would it be a reference to the plenary session of the party or the Assembly session?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Assemblies, Municipal Assemblies, discussed decisions of state authorities, state agencies, whereas the party discussed its party affairs. So if it was a document of the Assembly of the Serbian People, then it could be a subject of discussion at the municipal level. If it was a party document, then it would be discussed by party organs at the municipal level.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us something about Crisis Staffs. When were they established? Was there a Crisis Staff at the level of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Were there any Crisis Staffs in Croatia? And what is a Crisis Staff in essence?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Crisis Staffs were presented before this Court, Your Honours, as an important document. In the former communist regime, in every situation of natural disaster, any extraordinary circumstances called for the establishment of a Crisis Staff. There was one Crisis Staff at the level of Bosnia-Herzegovina headed by Ejub Ganic. The Presidency had its own Crisis Staff. So it was not a -- something prohibited. It was something that was triggered by certain circumstances. When I was Speaker of the Assembly, a Crisis Staff was formed at the time of the barricades in Sarajevo, when a member of a wedding party was killed in Sarajevo; a Crisis Staff was formed then. The leadership was away in Geneva at negotiations and neither Mr. Karadzic nor Mr. Koljevic nor I were there. It was a one-off Crisis Staff. Crisis Staffs did not exist then on the Serbian side. The first instruction to establish Crisis Staffs came in the speech of Mr. Karadzic on the 27th March, at the last pre-war Assembly session, when he said: Form Crisis Staffs, engage people from your own territories, and you will see from the records that it was the first mention of Crisis Staffs on our side. Whether some people formed Crisis Staffs at municipal level, I don't know, perhaps they did. In any case, they were able to because they didn't need any approval or instruction. It was quite a normal thing in the socialist system. If a river flooded, if there was any natural disaster or an extraordinary occurrence, Crisis Staffs were formed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You just spoke about municipal Crisis Staffs. Was a political party able to form Crisis Staffs without you knowing, considering that a political party is not a state authority? Were there any party Crisis Staffs before the 27th March?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: I believe I would have known if the party had done that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who, and based on what criterion, became a member of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: I remember that in your speech of 27 March you said that a leading person in the municipality should be the president of the Crisis Staff. That was the initial instruction. I don't know if anything was done about it, but very soon, the government of Republika Srpska issued some sort of instructions along those lines as to who should be on the Crisis Staff, the president of the Executive Board or maybe the chief of police, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did it specify personalities or titles, posts?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Exclusively posts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At that Assembly session of the 21st December, did the Assembly adopt a decision to establish the Serbian Republic of BH and did it set any conditions? Was the establishment of the Serbian Republic of BH inevitable? What demands were made from the other two sides?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Your Honours, as you will see in the transcript and in the record, it was said clearly: You, gentlemen on the other side, withdraw your unlawful decision, take back your request for international recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and if you do that -- if you don't do that, by new year we will have established the Serbian republic. And that was in accordance with the indications given by the international community that we will get our own entity by the Serbian new year, which is the 13th/14th January. That was the dead-line they had to take back their unlawful decision and their unlawful request for recognition.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And how much time did we give them? That is to say, when was Republika Srpska proclaimed and did it begin to operate immediately? When did it begin to operate?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: I had in my possession some documents, and, Your Honours, you can find them too, this declaration or the proposal of a decision, where we requested that it should be conditional. Once again, you'll see that it was a proposal and conditional that, on the 9th of January, we would set up Republika Srpska, but if the unlawful decisions were withdrawn, we would withdraw this too because we wanted to give one more chance. There was much pressure from the deputies, and eventually Mr. Karadzic, Mr. Koljevic, and I, we were in the minority even because the deputies said: Here's the interview saying -- showing what Mr. Izetbegovic said a few days ago, and those from the other side, they will never withdraw it. They want to go towards independence, and any request of yours is even comical. You are knocking at an open door and you know that nothing will come of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you now try to remember the events of the 9th of January, the proclamation of Republika Srpska, and whether its organs began to operate immediately or when did that happen?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: The 9th of January was actually a ceremony. We wanted to announce this so that it would be clear that we didn't agree with the unconstitutional decisions. We were hoping that the positions would get closer. You'll see that on the 25th and on the 26th of January, with much insistence from Mr. Karadzic, Mr. Koljevic, Mr. Vuka, and myself, we managed to persuade the deputies to attend the joint session of the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina, hoping that there would be a reconciliation. And automatically, everything that had been previously formed was annulled. And then there was a comical situation where Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Cengic stood on the platform at the same time. I tolerated that too just to achieve the reconciliation. So there was no implementation at all because we were hoping that negotiations and a political solution that would be in accordance with the constitution would ensue and would take into account the will of all three ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You now told us what was going on in the joint parliament on the 24th and the 25th of January, 1992. Could you please tell the Chamber what was it that Mr. Muhamed Cengic and I agreed on and kept agreeing for two or three hours? What was his proposal and what was my reaction to it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: As we kept insisting on the following - the Serbian side, I mean - if we wanted Bosnia-Herzegovina to be recognised as an independent country and for us all to vote at a referendum, then Bosnia-Herzegovina would need to be transformed, decentralised. A number of autonomous areas should be established where our and their and all other requests would be met at a minimum and no one should rule any other ethnic group. There should be no out-voting. We had long discussions about this, and at one point we were actually discussing more outside of the parliament session than at it. So when we were in these other rooms, an agreement was reached between Mr. Karadzic, Mr. Izetbegovic, Mr. Cengic was present, so was I, and there were other representatives too from all three ethnic groups. I have to be honest, the Muslims and the Serbs were there. As the Croats, they did not want to be involved then for some reason, I don't know what. It was more a conflict between the Serbs and the Muslims. And Mr. Izetbegovic then agreed. He said: I accept. We should implement a quick regionalisation in a short time and then we would all vote at a referendum. In late January or in March we would have a referendum. Once we conducted the referendum with our recommendation that Bosnia and Herzegovina should be an independent country, then the tensions would ease off. And Mr. Cengic then entered the main hall and presented to the parliament what agreement was achieved in the other office. While he was speaking, simultaneously Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Cengic were on the platform. Cengic had stepped down from the platform and Karadzic remained on it, and Karadzic said: I'm happy, and whatever Mr. Cengic says is correct. Our positions have become close now. We should implement the regionalisation. And then Cengic came to Karadzic on the platform, you can see it from the video recording, and then both of them said: Look, the situation is relaxed now. There is no need for tensions now. The government will implement the regionalisation quickly and the problem will be solved. I could see everyone in the hall relax and I was really happy. At that moment there were reactions of some of the deputies to the effect: Who did you agree with, Mr. Cengic, who entitled you to do that? And then he said: Well, here Mr. Izetbegovic agreed to that, and he pointed his finger at Izetbegovic. Then the president of the Deputies Club from the SDA requested for a break. They went to the break. He talked again with Mr. Izetbegovic and he said: This is not true. I do not accept this. And he cancelled what Mr. Izetbegovic had said. And then there was another chaotic situation, another rift. Once again we submitted the 20 signatures, once again the decision was adopted, and so everything started going downhill though we were close to find positions that were close to each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned that as early as in 1991, Mr. Vance and Lord Carrington and Mr. Wijnaendts came and others that you wrote to. Can you remember when it was that agreement was achieved in principle that there would be three Bosnias and that the work on harmonisation of the document began?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: I won't be specific. Whether it was during January or in February, early February, but immediately after this a meeting was organised at which it was told to us that we would have our own constitutive entity within Bosnia and Herzegovina. So immediately it was middle -- in the middle of January or late January or early February and then the negotiations and the conference were continued.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember whether you attended the plenary session of the Serbian Democratic Party held on the 14th of February, 1992, when we announced that there would be three Bosnia and Herzegovinas? And do you remember my recommendations what our leaders should take into account vis-à-vis the Muslims and Croats in the areas where we had the majority population?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: From this distance in time, I just remember what is positive. I very often tend to and try to forget what is negative. You can find that in the transcript; it's easy to establish. Mr. Karadzic appealed on everyone to protect -- if there is a demarcation line drawn between the three entities, if one of the ethnic groups is a minority in our entity, the Muslims or the Croats, we wanted to have a rule of law, we wanted to have the minorities protected with all rights to be enjoyed. And if anything like that happened, it could only be by somebody's will if anyone wanted to leave. Nobody should be forced to leave. Whatever was said then was easing the tensions. People were relaxed and it was the basis for the next session of the conference where we would advocate the position taken by the members of the plenary session, and their position was that now we had to adjust to new goals which were no longer Yugoslavia but rather Republika Srpska, a Serbian entity within Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I do not have your judgement. Is it true that it contains the adjudicated fact which is more or less to the effect that on the 14th of February, Karadzic said that Serbian political leaders should make sure that there was no exodus from our areas, and that the conclusion of your Chamber was that at the time I still made sure that the interests of the Muslims and the Croats would be protected?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: That's true. It's correct you appealed on everyone to prevent an exodus and that no one had the right to force anyone out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So that was two weeks before their referendum was held. Can you please remind us and tell the Chamber, what was our position with regard to this referendum and whether we would vote in it or not, and also what we thought about their right to state their mind?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Everything that I'm going to say can be found in documents. The clear position of the Serbian Democratic Party was that this referendum was, for us, a referendum of the Croatian and Muslim peoples. The Serbian people had voted at the plebiscite and said what they believed. Those who wanted to vote at the referendum, even Serbs, should not be obstructed. Everyone was entitled to vote because no one prevented us from holding our plebiscite. It was rather a written document sent out to the field so that people would know that no one had the right to obstruct anyone in the areas that was solely populated by Serbs if this referendum was to be organised there, if it was to be slated by the Muslim and Croatian communities, because it was not like a parliament session, it was slated in an unlawful manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you remember, of the 109 municipalities, from how many municipalities did we have deputies in the Chamber of Citizens, or rather, in how many municipalities did we have absolute majority?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: I could not say what the percentage was, but I know that in many of the municipalities the Serbs had absolute or relative majority. And why? Because the Serbs possessed land in big areas, and where municipalities were centred in urban environments, there the Muslims and the Croats had the majority, so that in a great number of municipalities the Serbs were dominant. I think, but whatever I say will be speculation. But I know that it was a huge number of municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that in the Chamber of Municipalities we had more than a simple majority, that is to say, 37 deputies? And who was the president of the Chamber of Municipalities?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: That's correct. In the Chamber of Municipalities we had the majority because -- and that was why we also had the position of the president. A Serb, Mr. Petko Cancar was the president of the Chamber of Municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In view of the fact that you were the parliament Speaker and also the president of the constitutional commission, can you tell me whether this referendum of theirs would be considered successful if in the 37 municipalities we prevented its -- prevented it from being held?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: All decisions are made autonomously in one and the other chamber, and if we were to look at municipalities separately, first the decision will have to be made in the Chamber of Municipalities, then in the Chamber of Citizens, and then such a decision would be passed at the level of the parliament as a whole. The Muslim/Croatian coalition could not even in theory secure for itself a two-thirds majority if all the Serbian deputies were to vote in the Chamber of Municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Perhaps I was not precise enough. This legality of the referendum, what it would look like if in the 37 municipalities and in -- I don't know which percentage of the territory, the Serbian side prevented the referendum from being held where it was capable of preventing it? Would the referendum then be considered successful?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: For the international community which expected to get the results of the referendum, it certainly wouldn't be acceptable and legal because there would be more than 51 per cent of the territory where the results of the referendum would not exist because the citizens would not be able to vote.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Immediately after the completion of the referendum, as you noted, one member of the Serbian wedding party was killed in Bascarsija. This was followed by unrest and the barricades were put up. Where were the two of us at the time? I believe that you mentioned that we were in Brussels; however, it seems to me that we were at the preparations for Brussels in Belgrade. Do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: As far as I remember, we were at a session in Brussels or in Geneva, and on the way back from that meeting to Belgrade, we heard about the barricades being put up and the murder of this member of the wedding party. We may have been in Belgrade, I don't know, but when this was happening we were in Belgrade in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That was the beginning of March. Can you tell us how did the conference develop and who presided?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: In March, Mr. Cutileiro was very active and very busy. He was the Portuguese ambassador who at the time, I believe, was in charge of the European community. At the time, Portugal was the presiding country. And March is the month of the finalisation of negotiations when we were about to achieve some results. Unless I'm mistaken, we had two meetings and we reached an agreement on the principles in accordance with which the final agreement about peace in Bosnia-Herzegovina would be based.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember what was the first map of Ambassador Cutileiro where he established who had the majority where?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: I remember that well. All three sides in the negotiations with Mr. Cutileiro mainly kept asking this question, but the map, the map, the map, and the map, because territorial issues were the most important for reaching an agreement because three constitutive units were to be set up. And then the late Mr. Darwin drew a map where he identified certain areas with relative or absolute majority of -- for one ethnic group. So, to give an example, you have a bigger enclave --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have 1D03931 called up because it will be easier for the witness to present this for us, 1D03931. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you recognise this? Is this the map you spoke about? Can you tell us what it depicts?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: During my trial, I tendered this map to the Prosecutor present here and he tendered a different map to me. This map was after the meeting on the 31st of March or around that date. As far as I can remember, after Brussels. That was the first time that the border was marked on the Una, which was the basis for our six strategic objectives.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. Could you please show the Una River to the Trial Chamber here?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: I'll try.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could he please be assisted with an electronic pen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I can manage. This is the border on the Una --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You can mark it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. That is the border on the Una. The green is Muslim territory and the blue is Serb territory. You see this here --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could that please be erased.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you precisely mark the Una River using that pen.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now could you please mark the Una River very precisely all along.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: This is the Una River. Sorry, yet again -- I haven't really managed. Sorry about that. I do apologise. I'm not very precise. The border between the green and the blue is the Una River. The Una River flows this way, as far as I can remember. This is the first time within Bosnia-Herzegovina that a demarcation was set between the Muslim - this is the Muslim area - and the Serb area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The Cyrillic S.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It looks like Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sorry. Can you go all the way down the Una to its confluence to the Sava.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: This is the Sava, this. This is the Sava up here, and the Una flows into the Sava, you see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In anticipation of the six strategic objectives, who was here on the Una River, on the right bank of the Una and the right bank of the Sava?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: What is marked here in blue --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. I have refrained from repeated objections to leading questions, but I'm going to be more rigorous now. In anticipation of the -- I mean, this is a clear leading question and building in commentary as well. Dr. Karadzic has to refrain from that and just keep his questions open-ended to this witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is your question, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me not mention the objectives. Can you tell me -- actually, can you extend the border along the Sava, and could you tell us who is on the right bank of the Una River and on the right bank of the Sava River on the basis of what was established by the team of the European Commission?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: I'm going to start from here, when the Una enters Bosnia-Herzegovina, that's this here. So the Una flows --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You've already said that. Could you place number 1 there.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: It is this here. From there, from that place, the Una flows towards the Sava. On the right-hand side --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sorry, number 2, could you mark the confluence with a number 2.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: That is number 2. On the right bank of the Una River, this is the Serbs, S, Serb ethnic area marked in blue. And on the left side, the green colour, that's where the Muslims are. This here is an enclave, if I can call it that, right here. One-third is brown or red and two-thirds are green. Croats are where it is brown. So this is where the Croats are. And these are the Muslims here. So I'm going to place number 3 there and the Muslims will be 4. The representative of the European community envisaged the following. Within a larger ethnic area, there can be enclaves of the other ethnic community. Of course, if you look at the principles, what is envisaged is even exchanges of territory, if I can put it that way, in order to satisfy a particular geographic or economic entity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you mark the Drina River for us now, where it flows into the Sava River, so that you don't have to deal with all of it.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Here, right here. Sorry about that. Number 5, that's what I'm going to put there now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you extend it a bit, the Drina, so that we see where the Drina is there?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: I'll try yet again. This is where the Drina flows. The Drina flows here. I think -- well, I don't know exactly. I think it's like this. Now I don't know if I'm being very precise, but I think it's something like that. Actually, I beg your pardon, it does enter Montenegro, the Tara and the Piva rivers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Number 6 for the Drina.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: I will place number 6 there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you mark the Neretva River approximately?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: The Neretva should be here roughly. I think that it's something like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Sorry, this is number 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is number 5?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Number 5 is where the Drina flows into the Sava.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please could you initial this or sign this and place the date there.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Only if I knew what the date was today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The 7th of November.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Before the break, bearing the break in mind and for as long as we still have the map there, could you tell us whether the paper called "Six Strategic Objectives" has anything to do with these boundaries of the Serb ethnic area?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: This map is a basis for rounding off or for creating the six strategic objectives.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this into evidence. Actually, another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We see here close to Banja Luka there should be a canton, or rather, an enclave Muslim/Croat. What about the Drina valley, Podrinje, who is there?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: If you look at Podrinje, the Drina River valley, it is this entire eastern part of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The green colour are the Muslims here. These are the Muslims and these are the Serbs. So maybe I should put some numbers there. I don't think it's necessary. Then green is a rather large area in the Drina valley and it was supposed to be divided between the Muslims and the Serbs. The Muslims would have these enclaves, so to speak, and the Serbs would have these areas that can sort of visually be linked, Semberija, Romanija, and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted and can we take the break then?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit Number D3998, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll have a break for 45 minutes and resume at 25 past 1.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.37 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Excellency. Once again could we have the map, please, 1D03931. This time an unmarked one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, we saw the decision, or rather, the recommendation of the Serb Assembly, the Assembly of the Serb People, to establish Serb municipalities.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be assisted with the electronic pen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether these ethnic boundaries, the boundaries of these ethnic areas coincide with the municipalities of the -- with the borders of municipalities or is there a difference?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: These ethnic areas do not coincide with the borders of municipalities in the areas where the two colours, if you will, of ethnic areas - how do I put this? - where they meet. I can give you an example. Right here --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please do draw what I'm going to ask you to draw. Do you see the municipality of Bihac?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: I see it, it's right here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please draw all the areas that are encompassed by the Bihac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: I hope that I will do this right. This is the municipality of Bihac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If a Serb municipality of Bihac is established, what does it include?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: If a Serb municipality of Bihac were to be established, it could include -- well, I'll try now, this area that is blue. Right here, that's one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about a Muslim municipality of Bihac, what would that include?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: This area. Muslim municipalities. So what is marked in green and that is within the boundaries of the overall municipality of Bihac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about the southern part that is left out, is that the municipality of Bihac as well, to the south?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Well, possibly. I'm not very precise, am I? Maybe this part is included by Bihac too? I was not precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Green, green.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Possibly. Possibly. All of this might be Bihac, that is to say, this area, green, that's Bihac, just like the blue one over there. But of course, the blue denotes the area populated by Serbs, whereas the green denotes areas where the majority population is Muslim, so not the entire population, the majority population is Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you mark the boundaries of Bosanska Krupa now. What does it include?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Now, Bosanska Krupa, I think that this is Bosanska Krupa. Actually, could it be blown up a bit, this map. I'm so sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. We lose the drawing. However, perhaps no harm done in blowing it up and having the drawing repeated so that it could be more precise.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Maybe I could take the liberty of saying -- well, sorry. Maybe this could be Bosanska Krupa, maybe this, so this part here, if my drawing is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was Bosanska Krupa on the left bank of the Una as well?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Certainly. Well, this is a free drawing because I'm not precise, but it was on the left side too. Maybe I can do this free drawing and then there is part on the right bank of the Una too. One were Serb areas and the other Muslim areas, and the Una went through the municipality of Bihac and the municipality of Krupa.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If Serbs establish a Serb municipality of Krupa and if Deputy Vjesnica [phoen], after the beginning of the war, says: In the Serb municipality of Krupa there is not a single Muslim and I hope that there never will be one for as long as the fighting is going on, which part of Krupa is he referring to?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: He is referring to the Serb part of Krupa, which is predominantly populated by Serbs, or rather, Serbs are an absolute majority. So in that part of the municipality where the Serbs are a majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, please, this Muslim enclave, do take a look at it. Does it include Kljuc, Sanski Most, and part of Prijedor? Which municipalities are we sharing with the Muslims and Croats in the Sana River valley? Could you please mark this in blue -- no, red, red. Could you mark the Sana River from Novi Grad to Prijedor to the south.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: I think here, because you cannot really see it so well, I assume that the Sana River, Novi Grad, that Sana is here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, it has to pass through Prijedor, so can you please take a look at that.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Well, I can't see it. Yes, it does flow through Prijedor and then enters Novi Grad -- ah, excuse me, Sana is here from what I can see. I think that's it. It passes through Prijedor. This is Prijedor here; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And were these municipalities ethnically homogenous or have ethnically homogenous parts and were thus divided between the Serbs and the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: This image shows that there was a division of these municipalities between the Muslims and the Croats, Krupa, Prijedor, and Bihac, these ones that we mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And the Croats?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Yes, the Croats. It's just this part. This area marked in brown is Croatian, this brown area here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I now please ask you to draw in the outlines of the Zvornik municipality and to tell us what made up the municipality of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Krajisnik. I'm not sure whether -- if we would be assisted if we look at this marked map later on. Why don't we re-draw it. Just zoom in on the western part and then let's draw these three drawings again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And let's do it separately with Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, and as long as the Court has stopped this for a moment to ask about its utility, may I ask what precisely is the underlying utility of having this witness guess at municipal boundaries which can be identified on a number of much more reliable documents that we have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think that this is -- the purpose of this exercise is not to find out exact border of municipality, but -- let's zoom in it first on the western part. We can ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: His Excellency, Judge Kwon, is right. We can just sketch it. It doesn't have to be precise. All I'm interested in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's zoom it one further. Further. Upper part. Yes. First, could you draw the border-line of Bihac first.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Now this is much more easy to see. This is Bihac. I will try to indicate that. I think this too. This is Bihac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Number 1 for Serbian part.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Number 1, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Number 2 for Muslim part.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And now with black pen, could you mark the Bosanska Krupa.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is Krupa from what I can see, this is Krupa. I don't know whether it's that part at the top, but from what I can see, Krupa is this part here. Probably it's like this as well. This is Krupa, 3 is the Muslim area, and 4 is the Serbian area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And what did you ask, Mr. Karadzic, to Mr. Krajisnik, Sana River? What did you ask next?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked him to mark the Una River, but you can see it exactly. It's where these two lines or these two colours meet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please draw that line between that -- the Sana and then going through the Prijedor enclave. Perhaps you can draw that line as well.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Well, I think this is the Sana. The Sana flows through Novi Grad, it passes through Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does it pass through Sanski Most and close to Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: It passes through Sanski Most. This is Sanski Most. And it passes through Kljuc, yes, it passes through Kljuc. Yes, this is Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now can you please mark in blue, let's say, Sanski Most, the municipality of Sanski Most, its borders, because it's already partly marked.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: This is Sanski Most. This is Sanski Most. Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please mark the Serbian part with the number 5 and the Muslim part with the number 6.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Well, perhaps we could mark Prijedor first because I marked that as well. Well, all right, 5 is the Serbian part and 6 is the Muslim part of Sanski Most, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please indicate the boundaries of the municipality of Prijedor and mark that.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Sanski Most --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Ah, Prijedor. Well, from what I can see, I think this is like this -- no, no, excuse me. This is Prijedor. I don't know if I'm precise enough. Perhaps I went too far a bit this way, but more or less, this is the area of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you mark the Croatian part with a number 7, with the number 8 the Muslim part, and with the number 9 the Serbian part of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: 7 is the Croat part, 8 is the Muslim part, and 9, 9 is the Serbian part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since we're unable to zoom in and out, could you please date and sign this map. And could you please tell us if there was a recommendation or the possibility -- it's not 2011, I'm sorry, it's 2013.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If there was a recommendation to form two municipalities, could you please tell us what one of them would consist of and what the other would consist of. Could you use Bihac, Krupa, Prijedor, Sanski Most, and Kljuc as examples, please.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: According to this map, those who would be forming the Bihac municipality would go out and make the boundaries out in the field, but the normal thing would be that this part marked in green, that part would be a Muslim municipality of Bihac. This part marked in blue should be the Serbian part of this municipality. Since Una flows through Bihac, then it would be normal for the right bank settlements -- the area to the right of the Una belonged to the Serbs and the area to the left of the Una would belong to the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. And what would remain as common territory at the level of the town of Bihac; i.e., how many of our towns are parts of different municipalities and how many of them are just in one municipality?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Well, I could say that a large number of municipalities could be formed like this. There are examples, though, where it was just the area of one municipality where the authorities, the power would remain in power because it was made up of representatives of citizens who are inhabiting that area. Here everybody would have their own territory but there would be joint functions as well. The best example would be Bihac where the joint power or municipal structure could remain intact, but also it could be separate, it could be divided, if that is what they agreed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If one were to say or make a recommendation that Serbs, Croats, and Muslims in Prijedor formed their own municipalities within that single town, what would be part of one, the second, and the third municipality?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Well, this is the Prijedor area, if I was precise enough. So that area, let's say, of the Prijedor municipality could be that area coloured in brown. And number 7 could be used to form the Croatian municipality. This area marked in the colour green would be the area where a Muslim municipality would be formed. The area in blue is where a Serbian municipality could be formed. As you can see here, at the edges of this brown-coloured and the blue-coloured territory we can see Prijedor. Therefore, it's possible that the boundaries of the municipalities would be in the town itself. There would be no walls or anything like that, but on one side of the street would be one municipality and another on the other. But there would be no formal boundaries. So each of the sides could establish power in that area inhabited by members of one ethnic community.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell us, after the war how the Dayton Agreements resolved the territorial issues in the municipality of Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: The municipality of Kljuc is a small part of the municipality -- actually, a small part of the municipality was assigned to the Serbs, that is, Ribnik, a smaller area. The bulk of the municipality, including the town itself, was assigned to the Muslims or to the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The boundary was drawn quite imprecisely. There are some areas that were assigned to one or the other entity, but that's how the border was drawn, whereby municipality of Kljuc was divided into two municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we move the image a little bit towards the east, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll admit this image as Exhibit D3999.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And can we now have the same map but can we look at the eastern part of it around the Drina River.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting, Mr. President, are you able to tell us whether it was unusual to have several municipalities in one town or not. How many municipalities are there in Sarajevo before the war?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: It's quite usual. All towns, especially large towns, have a number of municipalities. The town of Sarajevo itself had ten municipalities before the war, and today on the Serb side there are seven or eight and also more or less the same number on the Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we move towards the east, please, towards the right. This is fine. I think we can stop here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at the municipality of Brcko, please, and tell us the territories that comprise that municipality, the municipality of Brcko. And could you please tell us how many municipalities were formed during the war and after the war in the district of Brcko, that's what it's called today?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Well, there's a problem here because there are no municipal boundaries shown here, but I will do my best. All right. I'm going to try to do this now. I think that Brcko is here, the town of Brcko, and I think that the municipality -- there are no boundaries. Tuzla is towards the south. I think that it was like this, but this is just a very roughly drawn map. There were three municipalities: A Croat one, a Muslim one, and a Serb one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And was this something that was proposed even before the war or did this just turn out like that and was formed like this during the war?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: There were proposals for that before the war, but during the war it was actually implemented in practice, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do we see the entire municipality of Zvornik here so that we don't have to move the map? Can you roughly indicate the territory of the municipality of Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: The town of Zvornik is here, and now I'm going to just make an estimate. I can roughly indicate that it was like this even though it's a rough estimate. I think this is how the boundaries of the former municipality of Zvornik lay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And which territories comprised that municipality?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: This municipality comprised Muslim and Serb inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And who controlled these green areas of the Zvornik municipality during the war, to the west of the town?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: I think that almost at the very boundary or at the outskirts of the city, more or less here, was where the border was. A part was controlled by the Muslims and the other part was controlled by the Serbs. So this was controlled by the Serbs and this other part by the Muslims. This is the area controlled by the Serbs. I'm going to mark this. This would be the area controlled by the Serbs, this would be the area controlled by the Muslims, this would be the area controlled by the Serbs, and then this would be the area controlled by the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since we don't want to move the map so that we don't lose the markings, I would just ask you to sign and date this map, please.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what was the name of this area around Bijeljina before the war and during the war?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: This area here, this entire area, I can mark it, is called Semberija.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we tender this document, please, this is document 4000, a landmark.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, we'll admit it, Exhibit D4000.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now scroll up so that we could see the mid-Drina area and the boundaries of the municipalities' ethnic areas. A little bit more, please. Very well. This is good.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The Serbian territories are not clearly indicated in Bratunac so we won't dwell on that, but could you please look at the municipalities of, let's say, Visegrad, Gorazde. Perhaps you could look at the municipality of Visegrad and that area, then Rogatica, Gorazde, and Srbinje or Foca.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it well. Do I need to mark anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, please. Mark both territories.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Visegrad municipality, if I can see this well, should be here. The border, the boundary is not marked here, but since this is Rogatica, then the boundary should run this way. It's not very precise, but that's roughly it because this is Visegrad -- I think this is a bit imprecise. Rogatica should be -- and I apologise for my imprecision again. This could be -- I'm not sure. I think this could be Rogatica, this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Gorazde could be like this. Maybe it's even here on the other side. So this is Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, just a moment. Does Gorazde cross over to the Serbian part?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry, maybe. This is Cajnice. I'm saying this with a grain of salt because I'm not entirely sure. Gorazde is on both sides of the Drina River, the Drina River being here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And tell us what territory's covered by Srbinje, or rather, the name before and the name now is Foca?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: This is Srbinje. I think the boundary runs like this. This is Srbinje. So this is not Gorazde, after all, this is Srbinje. I can't see the boundaries clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Speaker, in these municipalities on the Drina, were the conditions in place for establishing two municipalities?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: In all of these municipalities, all of the prerequisites were there for forming both Muslim and Serb municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How did the Dayton Accords deal with the Gorazde municipality?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: We can see very easily that Gorazde is a place where part of the territory went to the Serb entity and another part to the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. A part of other municipalities was attached to Gorazde, actually, to create a corridor to Sarajevo, to create a bypass.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Srbinje municipality, or rather, Foca, did part of Foca remain within the Federation? Was it divided like Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Yes. It too was divided, and to this day there is a Muslim municipality of Foca, although the town of Foca went to the Serb entity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what was envisaged before the war? Without a war, how much would Muslims and Serbs hold respectively in Foca itself?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: The municipality would be divided into two --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's not -- I mean, it's a little too -- what was envisaged before the war? By whom? By what? This is kind of a free-floating abstract concept that can be lifted and applied anywhere. So more specificity is going to be necessary for this to be meaningful in any way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm wondering what is the point of this exercise.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will rephrase.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Speaker, before the war, were there any negotiations about transforming these municipalities into two municipalities each and what did these negotiations have in mind for Foca?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: There was several representatives from both ethnic communities in the Assembly, and I have information that they conducted negotiations between them about dividing the municipality into two municipalities, wherein the Serbian territories would go to the Serb municipality and the Muslim neighbourhoods to the Muslim municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: To what extent did Dayton Accords verify that? Did Ribnik really go to the Serbs? Did Sanski Most go to the Muslims? Did part of Zvornik remain in the Muslim municipality? And what about a part of Pale? Can you give us municipalities which the Dayton Accords sanctioned as transformed?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Looking at the map we can see that very easily. Most of the municipalities were divided along ethnic lines. I'll give you a graphic example. Before coming here to testify, I was departing from the Sarajevo airport. I was passing through the part of Serbian Sarajevo, and the taxi-driver told me: This is the ethnic boundary, and that's one street. On one side of the street is one ethnic community and the other ethnic community has the other side of the street. And I said: How come? And he said: Nobody really thinks twice about having it divided along one street. That's one example, but you have examples of another kind, like in Zvornik. Similar examples can be found in Kljuc, in parts of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I'm really at a loss where we are heading.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Excellencies, I have been charged by this indictment that I wanted municipalities to be divided, that is, charged against me as a crime, that I proposed or that it was effected by the war that Muslims were divided, as had been suggested before the war. I am looking into how the United Nations dealt with this same problem in Dayton, when they didn't have to shoot and all they held in their hands were pencils --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I don't think you were charged for wanting municipalities to be divided, but I'll leave it to you. It's up to you how to use your time. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. But as part of the joint criminal enterprise, one reason, although it's a contradiction, one part of the JCE for the removal of Muslims and Croats is the division of municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I ask you, Mr. Speaker, to put a date and signature here. You don't need to put in numbers because it's obvious from the colour of different areas.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This will be next Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D4001, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I shall now cite several adjudicated facts from your trial, from your trial judgement. Adjudicated fact 1915: [In English] "However, among the functions" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Adjudicated facts in our case cited from Mr. Krajisnik's case? Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the Krajisnik trial judgement, paragraph 49: [In English] "However, among the functions, the SDS assigned to the Bosnian Krajina community of municipalities was the organisation of its defence in times of war or imminent threat of war."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did the Serbian Democratic Party have any possibility or the right to grant this competence to the municipality of the Bosnian Krajina? Is this adjudicated fact accurate?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right.
