I considered whether or not to object to presenting the witness with the adjudicated fact rather than the basic issue and having him provide information about that in a non-leading fashion but decided, okay, we'll let the adjudicated fact be presented. But then I don't think the accused should start answering the question for the witness in the course of the alleged question proposed by suggesting reasons why, in his view, the adjudicated fact can be attacked by the witness. Let's try to keep it if -- I mean, it's already problematic under the circumstances, but to lead the witness in this fashion is unacceptable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This adjudicated fact says SDS assigned certain tasks to Bosnian Krajina communities of municipalities, and he questioned whether SDS has any possibility of the right --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- to the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Right. I mean, the question is not asking the witness to comment on that one way or another; it's focusing -- directing his attention to particular alleged aspects of the situation that the accused thinks can bear on the accuracy of the adjudicated fact. Given the fact that we're already presenting him with a fact rather than eliciting -- we're already presenting a witness who, for various reasons we know, identifies with the accused. Now we're presenting him with a fact that the accused -- it's basically telling him: I would like you to attack, if possible, and on top -- which I let go by, and now he's essentially telling him how to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And then, in your view, how should the question have been formulated?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: He can always say something to the effect of: Can you shed any light on this adjudicated fact? He could have started from the proposition: Can you tell us about the nature of the Bosnian Krajina community of municipalities and what its organisational components were, et cetera. I mean, there are various ways to do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now I see your point, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I could do that, but I'm only interested in the defence function of Krajina. Did it derive from powers granted it by the SDS as stated in the judgement? In fact, is this adjudicated fact accurate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But -- that's correct, but --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- however, the issue is much broader and I'll come to the other part as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- by putting your previous overture, it may be viewed as if you are feeding the answer to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll put it simply.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this adjudicated fact correct or not? And in either case, explain why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Because he did not have the adjudicated facts before him, could you read it again. I will read it for you. "... among the functions of the SDS assigned to the Bosnian Krajina community of municipalities was the organisation of its defence in times of war or imminent threat of war." Is this not correct?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm afraid it was not interpreted correctly and it's not correct in the transcript either. It's not "among the functions of the SDS," it should be -- [In English] "Among the functions that" -- it doesn't say "that," but "among the functions the SDS assigned to the Bosnian" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry. "... among the functions the SDS assigned to the Bosnian Krajina community of municipalities was the organisation of its defence in times of war or imminent threat of war."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judges, this adjudicated fact is not correct and I will explain why it is not. The Law on All People's Defence stipulated precisely that all municipalities are entitled to organise All People's Defence. The municipalities having that power -- another law which stipulates that they may associate, or rather, join into associations, by virtue of that law all the powers that one municipality has can be conjoined at the level of the association of municipalities. Now, in our case several municipalities decided to join the association of the Krajina municipalities, and you can see exactly from these laws why this adjudicated is not correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I asked you about the associations of municipalities. Based on whose will they were formed and were they established once and for all or were they subject to modification?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: In the times of socialism, communism, associations of municipalities were formed by virtue of directives and many municipalities were unhappy with the choice of association to which they were assigned. And their interests were not necessarily best served by that particular association. And generally speaking, there was always a desire to make associations based on economic interest. And even before the war, all these legal possibilities were used for political purposes. And had there been no war, these associations would never have acquired another dimension that can be misinterpreted and abused.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Adjudicated fact 1913: [In English] "During the first months of 1991, the SDS began to organise Serb-majority municipalities in Bosnia and Herzegovina into communities of municipalities, in some cases severing ties with pre-existing communities of municipalities." [Interpretation] Was this taken to be a sin of yours? Was this lawful? Were we allowed to do that? Could the municipality change the community it belonged to?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Less than a minute ago I said that many municipalities wished to join either one community or the other. This was certainly always a wish that was being expressed, but not a single municipality could leave a community and join another one without the consent of the Municipal Assembly. So everything that happened had to be based on a decision by the Municipal Assembly of a particular municipality. So this certainly cannot be ascribed to the SDS, that the SDS initiated that. It was people from that municipality, members of parliament, assemblymen, citizens, they could articulate their requests in a certain way. That was quite permissible, but there was a procedure involved for leaving one municipality -- one community of municipalities and joining another one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not hear the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "SDS party leaders justified the associations" of municipalities "in terms of economic necessity."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. I'm not sure --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure Mr. Krajisnik heard the question. But before we come to 1914 adjudicated fact, what was wrong with the previous adjudicated fact? The adjudicated fact did not deal with legality of that forming communities of municipalities. You said -- I'm asking Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I beg your pardon. Could you please repeat your question. How did you understand this? Maybe I've made a mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'll read the adjudicated fact, and then you tell us what was wrong with it. Adjudicated fact 1913 from your trial judgement, paragraph 48: "During the first months of 1991, the SDS began to organise Serb-majority municipalities in Bosnia-Herzegovina into communities of municipalities, in some cases severing ties with pre-existing communities of municipalities."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly these former communities of municipalities were being severed, but it was because of the will of the citizens on the ground. They couldn't have done that without a decision taken by a Municipal Assembly. If there was will to do that on the ground, then they could do that. It could be severed as is stated, or actually they could cut through one community. They could join another one. How do I put this? At first the entire municipality would have to move on to another community if there is a decision to that effect taken by the Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I still do not understand what was wrong with this adjudicated fact as I read it to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it wasn't a municipality that was being split, or rather, it wasn't a community that was being split. One municipality could separate from one community and join another community.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about the SDS --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This adjudicated fact does not mention a split at all or separation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, maybe then the translation is not good. It says here "split."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The severing of ties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh, severing ties. Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That's one. And the other thing I'm interested in is whether it was the SDS that started this and ordered that and organised that.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: It is very easy to establish who it was that did that. The SDS could not have done that, although that was a party that articulated Serb interests. It was people on the ground who decided depending on their situation right there where they lived. Different parties, different provenances.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. From a legal point of view, how do things stand if there is a republican law and a federal law which is applied if they are not harmonised? Which one has priority?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Federal law had priority.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to draw your attention to adjudicated fact 1918. I don't need to read out all of it. I can recount what it says. At any rate, municipal authorities were supposed to make sure that only Yugoslav laws were being applied, suspending the implementation of republican regulations, thus creating legal foundations for communication, co-operation, and the like between these municipalities and the Federation and its organs, like the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia -- actually, the Assembly of that Yugoslavia and the Federal Executive Council and so on and so forth. So can you tell us what our legal system had envisaged and whether this was impermissible.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: In the former system, republican and federal laws were harmonised. Federal law could not be suspended by applying only republican laws. That would have been unconstitutional, so federal law had to be abided by. It could only be changed at federal level. It could not be suspended by the republican Assembly or republican organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. A while ago I already asked you whether we could declare territories, Serb ethnic territories in Bosnia-Herzegovina to be an integral part of Yugoslavia. That is adjudicated fact 1946. Could we or were we supposed to declare that to be Yugoslavia? You said that that already had been Yugoslavia and was Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: At that moment, in 1991, Yugoslavia did exist and all of Bosnia-Herzegovina was within Yugoslavia. We did not have any need to say: This is Yugoslavia now and the others who have not expressed their views are not Yugoslavia. Perhaps this has been misinterpreted. Perhaps this has been written erroneously. In this area where the plebiscite was carried out, these people have voted in favour of Yugoslavia and actually that was the basis to show where the citizens had voted for a political solution within which Bosnia-Herzegovina would remain within Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Our solutions and our proposals, did they imply that what we were asking for ourselves --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: -- was something that we were denying others --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I mean, again we're heading towards a leading answer. I mean, if he wants to know what the implication was of a particular solution and proposal, he can ask that and find out what the witness has to say instead of continually suggesting to the witness the answer he wants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, sustained. Could you reformulate your question, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: One adjudicated fact, and I'm going to read it out to you, suggests that we were denying others what we had envisaged for ourselves --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, excuse me, that's a very transparently backdoor way of doing the same thing that I just objected to and that was sustained. So now he's interpreting the adjudicated fact for the benefit of the witness. Anyway, you can see what's going on. I object again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What adjudicated fact are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1947. It would be best if I were to read it out. I wanted to link it up to the municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did we deny them the right to establish a municipality of their own in places where we established our Serb municipalities?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: We did not deny that. And there are so many statements of mine and of other top people from the Serb leadership who said at the time everything that we are proposing, suggesting, actually we are allowing the others the right to do that. We are not imposing anything on others. You can check my statements and you will see that that was our policy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If the Trial Chamber allows me to do so, I'm going to read out verbatim adjudicated fact 1947 which speaks to the contrary. It will be interpreted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: "Which speaks to the contrary" was leading. But please read out verbatim adjudicated fact 1947.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: "If the majority in one municipality had voted to remain within Yugoslavia, the whole of that municipality would remain. Municipalities where the majority of the people had not participated in the plebiscite (and were, thus, presumably, non-Serb-majority municipalities), the SDS proposed to look at single communes or settlements; if local communes voted to remain, then only that community would be considered part of Yugoslavia, while the rest of the territory of the municipality would be allowed to join an independent Bosnia and Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So let me explain. What they are saying, this adjudicated fact suggests --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Wait --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: -- that we would not have allowed a local --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Objection. I'm sorry, I shouldn't say "wait." That's astonishing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, I will intervene. It's your trial judgement, paragraph 74. I don't think you need explanation from Mr. Karadzic. Can you tell us whether that part of adjudicated fact is correct or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judges, that is not correct and I can explain why it is that it's not correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please go on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two things are being confused here. One is stating one's views during a plebiscite, that is to say, the number of citizens from municipalities -- from a municipality that voted for remaining in Yugoslavia. This was not viewed in a territorial way because in one municipality, say, 60 per cent of the citizens can vote in favour and all of them can be within the city itself, whereas the other areas may have voted in favour of having a Bosnia-Herzegovina. Later on, like this map, that was a basis where you could see exactly where certain citizens lived, Serbs and Muslims. That was a basis for - how do I put this? - demarcation within Bosnia-Herzegovina. Out of 1.300.000, 700.000, how many were there, Serbs, together with Yugoslavs, the plebiscite just showed what the will of the Serb people was, how willing they were to stay in Yugoslavia. Now, what is creating confusion here and which perhaps - how do I put this? - contributed to this confusion was that subsequent activities in a way caught up with the plebiscite. Now, what are these activities? We know that 60 per cent from one municipality voted in favour of remaining in Yugoslavia, and then what is being spelled out in very precise terms is where the Serbs live, where the Muslims live, and independently of the vote a demarcation is made. So this fact actually sublimated two activities that have nothing to do with one another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Speaker. Do you remember that in peace time, before the war, some minority local communes voted in favour of joining a neighbouring municipality and that we always approved of that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: That did happen. I know, for example, in Skender Vakuf there was that kind of example. One local commune said: I don't want to be in one municipality, I want to be in another municipality. And these two municipalities actually agreed on that. This Dobratic, the one that would -- they would leave and the other one where they would go. For example, in Bijeljina also, Janja and Bijeljina, there would be two municipalities, if that's what we can call this initiative which was in the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina. However, it was not carried through.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now I'm going to stop with the adjudicated facts because that subject matter was already dealt with during the negotiations. Now, could you please tell us about this 18th of March, when part of the Lisbon Agreement was being discussed between the three parties?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Between the 17th and 18th of March, three delegations, the Serb, Croat, and Muslim delegations, had a meeting at a residence called Konak in Sarajevo. Then under the chairmanship of Mr. Cutileiro they agreed on the principles for resolving the crisis. Let me paraphrase by saying that, the crisis of Bosnia-Herzegovina. We agreed on the basis of these principles that we transform Bosnia-Herzegovina, that Bosnia and Herzegovina be reorganised into three entities on the basis of the census. There was a proposal for 1981 and for 1991, when other principles would be involved, geography, transportation and some other criterion that would supplement this first basic ethnic criterion. Then all three parties accommodated their views, and immediately on the next day, the 18th, we went before the Assembly and we asked our members of parliament to agree to the consent expressed by our delegation in view of these principles.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what was accepted at that Assembly and what remained outstanding?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: The principles were accepted and what remained was to work on the maps, and on specifying the authority exercised at central level and local levels. So the principals say that these principles and that map are the basis for further talks in order to reach a final solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'm going to put to you 2004, another adjudicated fact, from paragraph 124 of your trial judgement. I'm going to read it out verbatim. [In English] "In response to an invitation from Jose Cutileiro, international mediator, to continue the multi-party negotiations, the Bosnian-Serb Assembly unanimously rejected a draft of the constitutional arrangements in Bosnia and Herzegovina." [Interpretation] Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: That's not correct. It's a very well-known fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, in both our indictments it is alleged that you, on the 18th of March, said: Now we are going in -- now go into the field - and maybe it's I who said it - now go into the field to put into practice what we had agreed. Tell me, what had we agreed? What was it about?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: That's a reference to an agreement made the day before and no conspiracy is involved. I'll explain very briefly because that's a basis for my involvement in the JCE. I am collecting new evidence to prove that I was not a member of the JCE and that my participation was not substantial, and I found that evidence. It's video footage from that session where there is a difference between the transcript and what I actually said. I hired an agency that made an expertise, providing an expert report, establishing that I was talking about a previous meeting and not some underhand play. The word used was "fortify," and the Chamber concluded that I was calling people to arms to fortify our territories, whereas in our language "fortify" can also mean "consolidate," "determine," "establish." I was talking about consolidating an agreement, not calling people to arms to fortify our territories. And experts in the area determined that this was absolutely not a reference to what was concluded it was a reference to in my judgement, and I will be able to provide that evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So who made an agreement about what before our 18th of March session? Did Serbs agree on anything amongst themselves?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Three delegations, Muslims, Serbs, and Croat, and the representative of the international community had agreed about principles on the basis of which they would make a future agreement. There was no separate agreement of ours on any issue. I was referring to the agreement made the previous day with Mr. Cutileiro.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Speaker, you told us what remained to be agreed. Was it necessary to reconsider the already agreed things, such as constitutional principles, the principle of transforming Bosnia into three entities and such? Could we apply that on the ground or did that have to wait as well?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: What had been agreed at that meeting was agreed, and the principles were not subject to change. We could see that, you know, people can always go against an agreement but they were not supposed to be changed. We were supposed to continue work at grass-root level to see which peripheral areas would end up in which entity. The map that you will see in the transcript I referred to was based on the proposal of the Muslim representative who said that it's better to go into the field to see which territory belongs to whom rather than do that in an office. So establishing territories -- identifying, perhaps is the best word, identifying territories on the ground. Finding an arrangement that would enable Serbs to end up in the Serb entity and Muslims to go to the Muslim entity. It was allowed to make adjustments for villages in peripheral areas to join one entity rather than another.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now it was interpreted as "establishing territories," not "fortifying." Do you remember what Lord Carrington used to say very often: Stick to the principles. And he said it very often whenever somebody showed a willingness to go back on the principles.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: My English is not that good, but I know that he meant if something has been agreed, you can't start discussions from scratch. We can only continue from the point where we left off.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At that session of the Assembly, the words "take power" were also uttered. Do you distinguish in our language between the words "take over power" and "take power"?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Wait, wait -- what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Continually leading questions, and an obvious reflection of the fact that this -- the accused can't trust this witness -- even this witness to provide him with the answers he wants, but has to tell him those in advance here in court.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely not. I want to point out some linguistic problems because what was said there was "take power," whereas the indictment says "the Serbs took over power." I just want to ask the witness what was understood by "take power."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You could simply ask the witness what's the meaning of "to take power" in the transcript. But before we go there, in relation to the previous question about the 18th of March session, was it referred to in the indictment?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Many times.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think he's speaking of Mr. Krajisnik's indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Not -- but he -- Mr. Karadzic also referred to his indictment, both of our indictments. I couldn't find it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Many Serb -- [Interpretation] I am often admonished that I recommended the take over of power at that Assembly session and that the Serbs later took over power in these municipalities --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, no, no. I was simply asking whether it appears in the indictment, 18th of March session, or the agreement the day before.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it is stated in the pre-trial brief that I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- asked or demanded that our people take over power on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, I thought you were referring to the indictment. Shall we take a break or shall we adjourn for today. Mr. Krajisnik, we'll continue next week. As you know well, please do not discuss about your testimony with anybody else. Is it Tuesday or Monday? Yes, Tuesday. We'll resume on Tuesday morning at 9.00. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 12th day of November, 2013, at 9.00 a.m.
